Chiral SU(N) gauge theories, consisting of Weyl fermions and additional fermions, are examined to analyze their dynamics. An older suggestion by Bars and Yankielowicz to match the theory's 't Hooft anomalies with those of free fermions is revisited, resulting in novel constraints for the large N limit. Furthermore, new SU(N) theories with fundamental matter and additional fermions are proposed, where their low-energy behavior is precisely described by theories of free fermions. These new examples offer non-supersymmetric counterparts to established supersymmetric dualities, highlighting a significant advantage - they can be solved exactly using Monte Carlo simulations directly in the large N limit. Utilizing these simulations, scale inequalities are verified and new patterns of behavior are identified. Lastly, a significant aspect is that these non-supersymmetric dualities have a well-defined non-relativistic version, in contrast to their supersymmetric counterparts. An overview of relevant SU(N) theories with fundamental matter is given, along with an analysis of their duals. Ultimately, it is suggested that these theories may hold the key to resolving long-standing puzzles surrounding chiral fermions on branes, as well as non-supersymmetric theories with mobile D-branes. Additionally, a considerable portion of these non-supersymmetric dualities may be translated into an underlying string theory dual, possessing a distinct characteristic - the mixing of the string directions with the space-time directions. An example of this is the non-supersymmetric duals of the Z_N -symmetric theories, where the string direction is encapsulated by a homotopy group. Lastly, it is proposed that some of these non-supersymmetric dualities may also apply to theories consisting of Yang-Mills with matter in both the fundamental and adjoint representations. An initial analysis is conducted to confirm the matching of 't Hooft anomalies in such theories with those of free fermions in both the large N and large k limits. Furthermore, a non-supersymmetric dual has been identified for one specific theory of Yang-Mills with adjoint matter, offering a substantial insight into its dynamics. An outline of relevant non-supersymmetric dualities with adjoint matter is given. Ultimately, it is demonstrated that nearly all non-supersymmetric dualities, consisting of SU(N) theories with fundamental matter, can be translated into a well-defined string theory and that the supersymmetric counterparts can exhibit an intricate behavior of confinement with multiple phases, coupled with non-trivial symmetries, in both three and four dimensions.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. We thoroughly evaluated our approach on challenging financial risk assessment problems. The proposed model and FABE code are freely accessible through github and an executable version can also be found at the same location under the name ar-cfab-evaluator. We also present a relevant problem within this area of research which to the best of our knowledge has not been explored before, namely the solution of a constrained NP-hard optimisation problem, which in the general case is equivalent to solving a combinatorial optimisation problem in polynomial time, a problem we found to be particularly challenging. Additionally, we found that our framework has potential applications within other areas of computational science, particularly in modelling the interaction of biological molecules. Our model and FABE framework could be applied to efficiently evaluate the likelihood of paths in systems that exhibit non-deterministic behaviour. Our approach is also universally applicable to efficient model evaluation in graphical models as well as the structural aspects of molecular interactions, thereby constituting a general-purpose tool. Lastly we present a mathematical proof of the NP-completeness of the general case of our optimisation model, a challenge we found particularly hard. The code used to generate the figures in this paper is also freely accessible through github. Through a series of controlled experiments we thoroughly evaluated the efficacy of our approach, specifically by comparing it against the state of the art model in a diverse set of problems, thereby establishing a set of benchmark problems whose solution was computed with exactness, thereby constituting a reference point for future evaluations. Our model based on FABE has consistently outperformed the comparison model, specifically by achieving a significant speed-up in our experiments. In particular we found that our approach significantly outperformed the comparison model by achieving a significant up to 6 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments. Our work then presents a novel efficient framework

Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node and edge details in a flow chart. The framework's results reveal high levels of accuracy in synthesizing programs at a 66.4% rate and also demonstrate robust node and edge recognition at rates of 94.1% and 67.9%, respectively. Furthermore, program synthesis occurs in approximately 60 milliseconds. A set of 3000 distinct flow charts was used in the framework's training, which is comprised of various program templates with randomly distributed nodes and edges. The framework's efficacy is evident in its ability to accurately recognize complex graphical structures even in scenarios where nodes are densely packed. The framework was evaluated using two diverse metrics: node recognition and program synthesis. The framework's end-to-end training allows it to make predictive errors, where parts of a flow chart's structure are incorrectly predicted as part of another area's structure. An example illustrates the challenge of program synthesis occurs when a node's output destination is unsure, leading to disparate results. The metric also captures the complexity of interpreting visual specifications by demonstrating that even when nodes are easily identifiable, recognizing the overall structure can be a difficult task. Conversely, node recognition becomes a simpler task when the overall program structure is easily understood. A detailed analysis of the results is provided, including a breakdown of the program synthesis errors and a comparison with other program synthesis approaches. The framework's code is available for public use at a specified repository. A set of challenging flow charts is also offered for testing other program synthesis methods. The results reveal that deep models outperform rule-based synthesis methods in program synthesis, while a combination of models is the most effective approach when aiming to capture the most diverse programs. An exploration of models is conducted to identify the best combination of program synthesis methods. An experiment is also conducted to examine the depth of the deep models, revealing that a two-layer convolutional neural network is the most effective setup. An evaluation is also performed using real world datasets, revealing that deep models can successfully synthesize programs from visual specifications in a task called program transformation. The framework's results are evident in its program synthesis output, where over two-thirds of the generated programs match their intended result. An examination of the synthesized programs is conducted, revealing that deep models successfully create programs with desired properties

The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive opportunity for optical and near-infrared follow-up observations following the detection of GWs. The observation of a kilonova associated with GW 170817 from a Os-like isoelectronic sequence revealed signs of nuclear contamination not anticipated from initial model calculations, suggesting the necessity for more comprehensive atomic structure modeling. For the purpose of enhancing kilonova model predictions, a new set of relativistic atomic structure calculations for low-charge, medium-z ions has been constructed, featuring the Os isoelectronic sequence up to Os itself and including Au IV. Our latest paper utilizes the relativistic atomic structure approach called the Relativistic Atomic Structure Structure (RASS) to produce energy levels, E1, M1, and M2 transition data as well as a relevant line list essential for modeling kilonovae, with specific focus on the ejection velocity and temperature-sensitive transitions in Os and Au IV. Our analysis of the RASS data for Os and Au IV reveals discrepancies with existing non-relativistic structure calculations, tracking back to flawed orbital configurations which we rectify. As a direct outcome, our findings rectify earlier estimates of optical and near-infrared kilonova colors, specifically in the range from 0.5 to 2.0 $\mu$m, at various ejection velocities and temperatures, thereby contributing valuable data for future gravitational wave studies. Our work, in conjunction with the observed colors from GW 170817, strongly indicates the necessity of incorporating nuclear contours originating from neutron star mergers, necessitating further advancements in atomic structure modeling with the aim of incorporating higher-order processes. While this work addresses a particular instance, our improvements to the atomic structure sequence also initiates a new pathway for refining the opacity in diverse astrophysical settings, such as neutron star mergers, collapsars, and light curve peak stages. Consequently, this research will contribute to refining future kilonova model predictions and enhance our understanding of multimessenger astronomy events involving neutron star mergers. Moreover, our work initiates a new pathway for incorporating atomic structure sequence data, thereby facilitating future improvements in numerous astrophysical settings, such as neutron star mergers, collapsars, and light curve peak stages. Radiation oncologists' goal is to target tumors accurately while shielding surrounding vital organs, specifically the stomach and intestines, from x-ray beams. The incorporation of MR-Linac systems allows real-time tumor positioning, enabling precise radiation dosage adjustments based on shifting cell populations. The manual process of identifying these organs and calibrating X-ray beams can be lengthy, extending treatment times up to one hour a day, making automated techniques with deep learning essential. A recent paper explores the use of deep learning-based automation to streamline this complex task and provide faster access to treatment for a greater number of patients. The researchers employed a publicly accessible MR-Linac dataset, incorporating random transformations to create training and testing sets for a segmentation task involving stomach and intestinal identification. The model was evaluated using an IQ metric that measures similarity, and compared to a baseline human segmentation, revealing the advantage of deep learning-based automation. The success of this technique, and similar applications using convolutional neural networks, presents opportunities for improving clinical workflows and patient care. The resulting model can be applied in clinical settings, enabling radiation oncologists to target tumors more effectively and reduce treatment-related side effects. This paper is an adaptation of the authors' original work, titled "Automated GI-tract segmentation using Deep Learning", published in the proceedings of The International Conference of Medical Imaging Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention, 2021. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. We will illustrate the distinct aspects of compositional data analysis through a case study that utilizes a biochemistry dataset. The case study highlights the use of appropriate data transforms, the construction of variance-covariance matrices, and the interpretation of results in the context of composition data. Our approach focuses on logratios that are supported by statistical models, taking into account the dataset's zeros and limits imposed by its components' sum to 1. The lesson from this case study can be applied to researchers working with various types of compositional data. They can utilize the techniques outlined here to explore their datasets before performing analyses, such as linear regression or clustering, and interpret the results in the context of composition data. We employ linear algebra, visualization, and interpretation to convey this message. In particular, we show logratios as percentages or multiples of one another, and we illustrate how different composition data can yield the same set of logratios. A substantial portion of the material is new, and it has not been covered in previously published works related to compositional data analysis. The text is accessible to researchers who may not have a strong background in linear algebra. We use concise explanations and illustrations to communicate the unique aspects of compositional data analysis. The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a dominant process in shaping the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets according to core accretion theory. Given the MOA survey's focus on the super-Saturn mass range and this analysis extending to sub-Saturn masses, the CORALIE/HARPS dataset provides crucial insights into the transition from planetary to stellar mass objects, which may be influenced by factors such as core fragmentation, gas disk instability, or magnetic activity that could impede or halt accretion once a core reaches a certain mass. These findings may imply a rapid transition from planetary to stellar mass object formation, which could be driven by one or a combination of these factors, as well as the potential for massive sub-Saturn exoplanets to orbit closer to their host stars due to convective instability in the parent disk. References
Mayor et al. (2011) discovered a well-separated peak in the mass-orbital period distribution of the CORALIE/HARPS dataset, which was subsequently analyzed further. The analysis used data from  2011 with additional measurements from 2019, which consisted of 790 planets with known masses and orbital periods from the exoplanet database (ExoplanetArchive.org). The dataset was filtered to exclude planets with anomalous radial velocity semi-amplitude and orbital eccentricity constraints, which revealed a nearly spherical distribution of measured radial velocity semiamplitude versus mass (or density) on a logarithmic scale for sub-Saturn mass objects with close orbital periods. This result does not support the runaway accretion theory and instead suggests that core accretion may be replaced by other processes at the transition from planetary to stellar mass objects. Further investigation is needed into core fragmentation, gas disk instability, or magnetic activity that could impede or halt accretion once a core reaches a certain mass, which could account for the observed phenomenon.

Artificial intelligence models, modeled after biological agents, can regulate their awareness by restricting their input from the environment to minimize information overload.  A key consideration here is, can a limited perception of its surroundings by an artificial intelligence be efficiently utilized for task accomplishment. To achieve this, an internal mental map of its condition is developed which makes predictions about where it may need more information. We investigate how neutrino-nutrino interactions affect the stability of dark matter made up of neutrino-like particles. Assuming these interactions cause neutrino condensation, we examine two possible scenarios - where the universe's temperature drops below the condensation threshold and dark matter components become stable, or when it remains above the threshold due to symmetry breaking in the universe's early stages. In the first scenario, we find that neutrino-nutrino interactions significantly alter the stability of dark matter, allowing it to exist for a much shorter or longer time relative to the universe's age. In the second scenario, we determine the conditions under which dark matter can consist of neutrinos, and find that such dark matter can either disappear, remain constant, or increase in abundance as the universe evolves. In each of these situations, we calculate the resulting scaling of dark matter's abundance with temperature, and evaluate the implications for our understanding of dark matter's properties in the universe. Finally, we explore the potential for neutrino-nutrino interactions to be tested in experiments that study neutrino decay, and suggest that such experiments could provide further insight into the universe's composition. In particular, we propose that these experiments could be modified to look for signs of neutrino condensation, and that this could provide a more complete understanding of the universe's physics. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and thus inspired local masking, allowing task-independent predetermined graphs, even with sparse masks. We demonstrate that resultively learned masks outperform task-specific fully connected RNNs across multiple benchmarks, achieving this with significantly lower training data requirements, up to a 25 times decrease for some datasets. These findings indicate RNNs with mask constraints can bridge the gap with state-of-the-art models, showcasing the efficacy of biologically inspired constraints in deep learning. Consequently, we hope these findings will propel research into the neural basis of learning. In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the source and target measures to have different total masses, this problem becomes complex. Notably, it is known as the Kantorovich optimal transport problem, and its solutions involve two distinct values - $p$ and $q$. These values determine the exponents for the $L^p$ norm of the optimal transport plan, and consequently, themagnitude of the averaging weights in the pooled feature space. This new, transport-theoretic framework offers insights into global pooling and enables the development of more effective methods by exploiting variations in the optimal transport plan's $L^q$ norm. As a proof of concept, a new global pooling module based on this framework has been proposed, and it is shown that it outperforms existing global pooling methods on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lychtc/UTP. Experimental results indicate that the proposed module significantly improves model performance when used in conjunction with other advanced machine learning techniques. To validate the insights gained from this framework, it is shown that the Kantorovich optimal transport problem can be transformed into a linear optimization problem with specific constraints. By analyzing this problem, the structural relationship between global pooling, the primal-dual method, and the Kantorovich optimal transport problem becomes apparent. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Kantorovich optimal transport problem can be viewed as a generalization of the equal variance problem in statistics, and new test datasets for evaluating global pooling methods have been developed based on this idea. The proposed framework provides a deep and comprehensive understanding of global pooling that can improve machine learning model performance. As an example, it is shown that the Kantorovich optimal transport problem can be used to develop new global pooling modules with predefined unit variance in the pooled feature space. Since the Kantorovich optimal transport problem can be transformed into a linear optimization problem, it is possible to structurally analyze the optimal transport plan and devise methods for efficiently computing its eigenvalues and prime factors. As a further extension of this idea, it is demonstrated that the Kantorovich optimal transport problem can be used to develop new global pooling modules with specified variance magnitudes in the pooled feature space.

The primary objective of this research is to address questions regarding the underlying structure of Active Galactic Nuclei, specifically their central black holes and surrounding engines, by examining the characteristics of a sample consisting of 351 AGN, which have been categorized into two types, Narrow Line Region and Broad Line Region Type galaxies based on their spectral features. Various statistical tests were applied to compare the distributions of key characteristics among these ARXIVcat galaxies, and after controlling for potential biases, significant differences were found in several aspects. Notably, the Broad Line galaxies tend to reside in larger, more massive host galaxies and are oriented at preferentially lower inclinations than Narrow Line galaxies. Additionally, there is a notable variation in the near-UV continuum shape across different Broad Line galaxy sub-classes, which may be an indicator of the role of dust in obscuring the nuclear emission. Our findings are consistent with previous studies and support models suggesting a link between nuclear black holes and their host galaxies. However, this research also highlights uncertainties and ambiguities in interpreting observed correlations, particularly due to limitations in data quality and sample size, and the influence of varying assumptions in orientation dependence. Future research should focus on acquiring higher-quality data and exploring other potential factors contributing to the variations seen among Narrow Line and Broad Line galaxies. Additionally, this research did not find supporting evidence for some previously reported differences and rather suggests that certain characteristics are a result of the underlying galaxy environment rather than distinct nuclear black hole properties. A detailed analysis of the data and its implications for understanding AGN and their host galaxies is presented in a follow-up research paper. In this initial study, the emphasis is on presenting the methodology and key results in a concise and easily accessible manner. A more in-depth examination of the research is available in a subsequent publication. This research also serves as a demonstration of how to effectively apply statistical tests to cultivate new insights when working with large comprehensive datasets. A comprehensive dataset, ARXIVcat, has been made publicly available in order to facilitate replication and further exploration of research findings. This research has significant practical and theoretical implications for understanding AGN and their potential as diagnostic tools for estimating galaxy and nuclear black hole properties. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training. Notably, although we were able
to bypass annotation during pre-training, it is indispensable for assessing our
proposed scheme's effectiveness. To validate our findings, we employed the
popular KITTI (outdoor) and NYU-V2 (indoor) benchmarking datasets and also
detailed the benefits and shortcomings of our pre-training protocol in relation
to alternative methods like unsupervised, self-supervised, and semi-supervised
training schemes. Additionally, we demonstrated the versatility of our pre-
training protocol by successfully applying it to models that had not been
initially designed for depth estimation. Our work's associated code and data
can be accessed via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/asharman/Depth
SE. In conclusion, depth estimation using monocular vision from video footage
provides a superior basis for pre-training semantic segmentation models. By doing
so, we are able to boost their performance when working with limited numbers of
annotated training samples. Furthermore, this method has been shown to yield
results comparable to those achieved through supervised training, thereby

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural model that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube uses a novel approach to data preparation, where the model learns to identify the most important aspects of the data and generates stories based on these key features. Through our experiments with various domains, including the evaluation of time-stamped event data and the generation of sales leads based on time-series data, we demonstrate that TCube outperforms other domain-specific methods in both automated and human evaluations. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of TCube in the field of earthquake research, where we use the model to create engaging narratives about the characteristics and behaviors of significant earthquakes. Our code for TCube is available open-source under the MIT License at https://github.com/jontaylor24/TCube. We also provide pre-trained models and demonstration notebooks at https://tcube-demo.jontaylor24.com. In a related project, we have also developed a suite of natural-language processing tools called TFlow that we use to prepare the data for TCube; this code is available at https://github.com/jontaylor24/TFlow. In a related thesis, we discuss the design and development of these associated technologies: https://jontaylor24.github.io/thesis. We hope that TCube, along with our accompanying documentation and public domain data, will enable other researchers to make the most of the great research ideas we present in this project. We especially hope that these contributions will facilitate new research in the domain of geology, where we have applied TCube to create engaging narratives about the characteristics and behaviors of significant earthquakes, as shown in the accompanying figures and results. We look forward to seeing the many great research ideas that we have enabled! This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. When utilizing the JUMAN parser, which is considered the traditional benchmark in Japanese word segmentation, KNP delivered a 95% accuracy score surpassing the established 94% benchmark set by JUMAN. Lastly, although this research primarily focuses on Japanese word segmentation, its underlying techniques and context are equally applicable to other challenging tasks involving Chinese character segmentation. As such, this study may also contribute to the advancement of Chinese word segmentation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them impractical for real-world applications. By leveraging a generic model, Flatee can be adapted to support different architectures, including deep learning models, through the representation of custom aggregation functions and mixing strategies. We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification.

This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive lens, demonstrating that certain properties within the cumulant-based ICA model can be captured efficiently using a smaller number of measurements than data dimensions. Building upon this understanding, this paper presents two novel algorithms, "Compressive Joining" and "Joining with Side Information, which utilize compressive sensing techniques to enhance the cumulant-based ICA spectral feature representation. Experimental results confirm that these algorithms result in a lower data-to-sensing ratio compared to conventional methods, and show significant reductions in computational cost with minimal performance losses. Three distinct applications - fMRI decoding, image analysis, and speech processing - are used to demonstrate the benefits of reduced storage and post-acquisition processing requirements without sacrificing accuracy. The study shows that decoding cognitive information from reduced fMRI data with side information leads to a significant reduction (up to 4 times) in storage and post-acquisition processing requirements without losing any accuracy. Similarly, low-bit rate image compression with joint side information can be efficiently achieved, cutting the total data size to about 9%. Additionally, reconstructing speech signals from reduced data with joining and side information yield nearly 1.5 bits per sample reduction in post-acquisition processing requirements. The findings suggest that future machine learning systems with deep learning-based tasks may significantly benefit from compressive sensing integration, particularly those involving cognitive processing, images, and speech, which could lead to size, power, and computational efficiency improvements (e.g., smaller, less powerful hardware, faster software processing). The work presents several open issues, such as generalizing the Joining and Side Information theory to other ICA models and exploring the use of neural networks as compressive sensing sensors. The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to resolve Asser's conjecture regarding the class's closure under complement, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.  We also note that, given a sufficiently large number $n$, there exist sentences $\Phi$ such that the largest possible model cardinality for $\Phi$ is less than $2^{n}$, yet the smallest possible model cardinality for $\Phi'$ is $n^{2}$, thereby establishing a gap between these two values.  We have found that this gap can be characterized by the notion of 'graph dual consistency', and we have identified a particular class of sentences whose model graphs exhibit this property.  We have further developed algorithms to determine graph dual consistency for specific types of graphs.  Using these algorithms, we have found explicit lower bounds for the complexity of determining whether a given sentence is true in all models with at most $n$ elements, as well as the complexity of creating a representation of a given graph using at most three variables. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's yield. Conversely, employing generative models can mitigate these drawbacks, enabling the creation of novel adversarial examples. Specifically, our analysis delves into the capability of generative models, particularly Variational Auto-Encoders, in creating adversarial examples. Our approach In our study, we introduce a new threat model, thereby setting the groundwork for future MitB research. Our findings demonstrate that employing a generative model can significantly reduce the number of malicious inputs required to breach DNN security, thereby increasing the attacker's yield. Moreover, our analysis reveals that VAE-based generative models can effectively produce adversarial examples in image classification datasets. Although the VAE model yields a lower success rate compared to query-optimization attacks, our study shows that it requires fewer interactions with the model. Notably, our results also show that using two VAE models can nearly match the security breach of query-optimization attacks, thereby increasing the attacker's yield. Our contribution In terms of contribution, we introduce a new attack method, marking the first instance where an generative model is utilized to create adversarial examples. Our study further demonstrates that the utilization of generative models can be an efficient approach to breach DNN models, thereby opening up new avenues for future research. Specifically, we identify two key factors that can enhance the effectiveness of these models: diversity-based decoding methods and double-freeze approaches. Our analysis reveals that these two methods can efficiently produce adversarial examples, offering an efficient approach to breach DNN models. Furthermore, our study also shows that the double-freeze approach can an match the effectiveness of query-optimization attacks, thereby offering an efficient attack method. Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies. Our approach can serve as a useful tool for understanding the spread of conspiracy theories within the context of social media platforms. Ultimately, this research contributes to the understanding of online misinformation that hinders climate change mitigation efforts. The data used for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/jbrennen/climate-change/tree/master/data. Additional material is also accessible at this site, including code for data analysis, the research dataset, and presentation slides. This research was inspired by a request from the National Academies of Sciences and Engineering, for which a summary of our findings is provided at the link mentioned above. In short, online conspiracy theories are not a significant threat to their spread, as mainstream media coverage appears to outweigh their online presence. However, their persistence has negative consequences, such as eroding public trust in established institutions, as well as among climate scientists and researchers. It is essential to document their dissemination on social media and distinguish it from accurate climate change information to better understand and combat conspiracy theories. This distinctness can be achieved by using stance detection and other techniques, such as tracking propagation patterns and user demographics. Conspiracy theories are not a unifying theme; they vary significantly, with some targeting specific groups, such as environmentalists, and others, like the theory that climate change is a hoax, which primarily spreads among right-wing users. Our research does not provide a comprehensive list of conspiracy theories but instead analyzes their dissemination online. We examined the most popular conspiracy theories and found that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Online platforms, like Twitter, can be used to monitor the spread of conspiracy theories by using stance detection and tracking propagation patterns. Our research contributes to the understanding of online conspiracy theories, their spread, and implications for climate change communication strategies. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results, particularly for blurry images and those with missing pixel values, outperforming existing state-of-the-art segmentation models. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion between luminosity and spin, and the potential effects of relativistic beaming, we determine the lower limits of the unified spin of supermassive black holes in a sample of 69 high-redshift, fast-luminous objects. Their spins are found to exceed 0.04 with 95% confidence, a value that exceeds previous findings. This research further explores the possibility that these high-spin black holes could be the result of the appearance of ultralight bosons through the superradiance process. The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Within a finite radius, the cloud is initially at rest, and we examine how mass accretes onto the black hole under two scenarios: with and without the influence of angular momentum. By solving the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in conjunction with a kinetic model, we derive a set of ordinary differential equations that describe how the cloud's properties change under these two conditions. Our analysis reveals marked differences in how mass accretes onto the black hole in the presence or absence of angular momentum, and we observe that the latter case exhibits convergence to the Bondi accretion rate in the cloud's infinite radius limit. Furthermore, a novel relationship is identified that governs how angular momentum affects mass accretion in the cloud's inner regions, and it is demonstrated that a kinetic treatment is essential for accurately describing this process, particularly at smaller radii. Ultimately, our findings offer insights into how a kinetic cloud's properties evolve as it merges with a black hole, and the potential implications for astrophysical black holes that grow through this merging process are considered. In particular, a black hole that forms from a kinetic cloud may possess unique features, such as irregular mass accretion patterns, as well as uncertain structural properties, such as irregular Roche lobe radii and unusual fundamental modes of oscillation. These characteristics, in turn, may give rise to distinct observational signatures, such as irregular variability patterns and unusual electromagnetic emissions, that could ultimately reveal the role of accretion in the black hole's mass assembly. A companion paper has already shown that a black hole that forms from a kinetic cloud will exhibit unique electromagnetic emission properties, and the current investigation provides further insight into its structural and dynamical behavior. In a third companion paper, the role of magnetic fields in merging kinetic clouds will be explored. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror. A special case of our framework, wherein the atom is bound above a hole in the mirror, yields a quantum version of the Landau theory for spontaneous emission. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5x1.5 degree square area, distinguished by their extinctions and Ks magnitudes.  Spectra from two extremely hot O stars show they are verified as O4V stars with masses exceeding 40 Msun.  Their velocity relative to the Westerlund 2 center, with respect to the star cluster, is determined as 112 to 169 km/s.  This supports the notion that both stars could have originated within Westerlund 2 and expelled due to dynamical interactions early on in their formation.  This study's findings are consistent with the theoretical predictions of massive star ejection in a dense star cluster environment.  The area around Westerlund 2 might hold many more O stars, with potential detection limited by the surveys' resolution and spectroscopic survey capabilities. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these drawbacks, researchers have proposed using deep learning in vehicular communication systems. Nonetheless, these deep learning-based estimators have been shown to have performance issues when working within real-world IEEE 802.11p systems. To resolve these problems, we have introduced a deep learning-based channel estimation scheme that incorporates an LSTM component, designed specifically for use in IEEE 802.11p systems. This novel approach leverages the LSTM's capacity to analyze sequential data, using only the IEEE 802.11p standard's pilot symbols for channel estimation. Through simulation, we have demonstrated that our estimator significantly enhances the baseline IEEE 802.11p estimator's performance, achieving an average channel tracking loss of less than 0.02 NaN meters in a diverse set of scenarios. Furthermore, we have found that our estimator performs optimally across a wide range of vehicles' speeds, with further improvements when combining our estimator with a temporal averaging technique. As a result, we have achieved an average channel tracking loss of as low as 0.01 NaN meters for even the fastest vehicles. With our estimator, vehicles will enjoy a reliable and efficient data transfer experience, even at high speeds. By employing the ANN's universal approximation property, we transform the networks in a way that ensures weight values are unique and easily computable. This weight determination method doesn't require ANN architecture parameters such as the number of hidden layers, number of neurons in each layer, transfer functions, or input/output data to be trained. Once the weights are calculated, the networks converge rapidly to the training data, achieving nearly perfect training accuracy within a brief time frame. This proposed approach offers significant computational benefits, particularly when dealing with large datasets and high-dimensional input/output data, as it eliminates the need for continuous network training and fine-tuning. This speedup is formally analyzed and shown to increase exponentially with the dimensionality of the data. Unlike previous weight calculation methods based on the ANN's universal approximation property, our approach can be easily generalized to solve non-linear projections and dimensionality reduction problems in complex high-dimensional data. This was not possible with previous methods, as they required iterative optimization and were confined to single-layer networks. In this study, we demonstrate that the weight calculation method can be efficiently used for solving difficult problems in high-dimensional data, such as reconstructing human brain images from single-electrophysiological recordings and modeling a living cell's behavior in a complex high-dimensional protein environment. Additionally, we showcase the versatility of our approach by generalizing it to solve other complex problems, such as the multiple-knot problem in signal processing and the multi-dimensional sorting problem in computer science. A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires knowledge of the causal relationships between features and target output. This information enables us to identify the parent and child nodes in a graphical model, representing features as random variables and a target output. We've developed a theoretical justification for our method, confirmed by experimental results showing improved performance on multiple datasets. Additionally, our method has been found to produce more realistic synthetic data when trained on unlabelled data in conjunction with importance weights. This is in contrast to the behaviour of standard semi-supervised learning models, which we've based on a generative model, named semi-generative modelling. The advantages offered by our method come from its ability to learn a representation that's invariant to certain causal variables while simultaneously producing synthetic data that's conditioned on the variables that it's supposed to depend on. This has given rise to a novel research area that we're terming semi-generative modelling, with the potential to significantly expand our understanding of how to learn representations while performing adaptation and generating data. In particular, we've found that knowledge of the causal structure can replace the need for knowledge of the underlying graphical model when training a representation, as well as the need for knowledge of the distribution of the target output when synthesising data. This has given rise to a new class of methods that we're terming semi-generative modelling, with the potential to significantly expand our understanding of how to learn representations, adapt to new environments and generate data, all while making use of unlabelled data and causal structure information. In this context, we've found that knowledge of the causal structure can replace the need for knowledge of the underlying graphical model when training a representation, as well as the need for knowledge of the distribution of the target output when synthesising data. Furthermore, we've found that semi-generative modelling has the ability to cover a wide range of scenarios that involve unlabelled data and causal structure information, effectively becoming a comprehensive and generalised framework for learning representations, adapting to new environments and generating data, all while making use of unlabelled data and causal structure information. Ultimately, we've found that semi-generative modelling has the ability to significantly expand our understanding of this challenging learning scenario.

Through thorough evaluations, Hamiltonian neural networks have achieved superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baseline models in multiple scenarios. Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2ℏ/R, where R represents the sphere's curvature radius, yielding countable energy and momentum spectrums for freely moving particles. A theoretical maximum for possible momenta in S^3 corresponds to its diameter, the de Broglie wavelength λ_R = πR. Building on this, the definitions and relationships for covariant position operators in terms of geodesic normal coordinates, along with commutator relations for position and momentum, are developed. As an extension, this research offers a unified approach to studying quantum mechanics on manifolds with a constant sectional positive curvature. Lastly, implications of this research for its extension to N=1 supersymmetric quantum mechanics are addressed. Preliminary findings for the three-dimensional hypersurface of M^4, a four-dimensional flat spacetime, are examined, revealing familiar results for the position and momentum operators, their commutator, and spectra. However, it's noted that these findings yield an unusual relationship between the spacetime's diameter and the de Broglie wavelength. Moreover, this research may enable novel developments in supersymmetric quantum mechanics. Areas for future research, such as its extensions to de Sitter space and superconformal theory, are identified. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our study demonstrates the efficacy of this approach by successfully simulating a two-dimensional Hubbard model at half-filling with ferromagnetic interactions, and we anticipate similar benefits for other sign-problematic models. Additionally, we showcase the potential of this method by achieving a ground-state measurement of the two-dimensional Hubbard model at a low temperature, with an error bar influenced by remaining statistical fluctuations due to the limited simulation size. Building upon this breakthrough, we envision extending our technique to tackle more intricate problems in quantum many-body physics. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub platform at: https://github.com/lomionne/neural-networks-for-qcd-and-qmcd.git. Furthermore, we have added a documentation file that outlines the step-by-step code implementation at: https://lomionne.github.io/neural-networks-for-qcd-and-qmcd.html. Lastly, the data generated during our study can be found at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9washington.2021.10387100.eyJ.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today. Further discussion and coordination among industry practitioners and policymakers are encouraged to join efforts in preventing the dark side of VPPM exploitation. The associated design concepts and this paper are made available under the CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license at the specified URL.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability, and it appears that using parallel corpora smaller than 1 million words significantly hampers model performance, underpinning the importance of obtaining high-quality datasets for effective model adaptation. Moreover, we identify the scaling approach as a crucial element, and we reveal that the method of adapting model embeddings to new languages has a substantial effect on adaptability, especially when adapting to languages with distinct writing systems, such as Korean. Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Furthermore, event duration is determined by aggregating consecutive time intervals with shared spatial areas. An added filter is incorporated to remove spam, false, or inaccurate events. The framework incorporates entity-based analysis to evaluate event credibility and reliability. Evaluation is performed using multiple datasets for distinct cities, including Melbourne, London, Paris, and New York, and is benchmarked against existing approaches utilizing clustering algorithms. Assessment of the framework is conducted using two metrics: f-measure and normalized intersection over union, with results showing significant improvement in accuracy and locality. For example, accuracy increased for Melbourne, London, Paris, and New York by 11, 10, 9, and 9, respectively. The corresponding locality improvements were 10, 9, 8, and 7 for the same cities. The proposed approach achieves an accuracy of 85% with 6 incorrect events (along with corresponding spatial and temporal offsets) among the top 10 events for each city. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed two diverse hyperspectral image datasets (sundials and railway tracks) that were collected using an hyperspectral camera, giving us a thorough understanding of the techniques from both a theoretical and practical perspective. Nonetheless, each of these methods has distinct shortcomings, including biased predictions of target classes with AE and incomplete recovery of pixels with DAE. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning. We will demonstrate that these techniques not only enable the creation of more compact models but also reveal previously unobservable structure within the networks, thereby providing crucial insights into how to develop more interpretable models. Our findings show that by employing continued pruning on pre-trained language models such as BERT, we can halve the model's size while maintaining at least 90% of its original performance. Furthermore, our models are approximately 1.5 times smaller than equivalent transformer models that were specifically designed to be compact in nature, and we have established that these improvements in size can be attributed to a substantial reduction in the models' layer complexity. Our work has also revealed that band-limited models, which are capable of performing well with band-limited filters, are preferred over other models such as the BERT model. In addition, we have discovered that knowledge distillation is an effective technique for developing more effective student models when employed in conjunction with continued pruning. Our contributions include establishing a new record for natural language models in terms of compression ratio while maintaining equivalent or above average performance, and we have provided the necessary code and models to allow for replication and evaluation of our findings. Our work has demonstrated the feasibility of applying the concepts of sparse networks and band-limited networks to the realm of natural language models, and in the process, we have achieved a new record for natural language models in terms of compression ratio while maintaining equivalent or above average performance. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for future research into the development of highly interpretable models through the application of sparse network and band-limited network techniques. ProCS predictions are found to be precise and within normal range for more stable protein structures, while less stable structures exhibit larger prediction errors. ProCS predictions are determined to be relatively insensitive to the density of coverage by NMR data, making ProCS a valuable tool for evaluating protein stability and refining protein structures, particularly for a wide range of moderately stable proteins. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Finally, a new proof of the Curry-Howard correspondence for intuitionistic propositional logic is offered, based on this equivalent form of the harmony condition. While this paper draws upon a specific proof theory framework, the proposed formulation of the harmony condition is likely to be recognizable as a common concept within proof theory itself. Nevertheless, the Computational Ludics framework provides a unique and insightful perspective on this formulation. Furthermore, the derived results are expected to be applicable not only to intuitionistic system but also to other structured proof systems. Specifically, an equivalent formulation of the harmony condition for classical logic, incorporating additional concepts from the Computational Ludics framework, is also presented. Although this derivation is inherently tied to the Computational Ludics framework, it is expected to yield notable results when translated back into standard proof-theoretic terminology. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. It's observed that agents can achieve similar levels of performance as those achieved through extensive comparison-based optimization, while significantly reducing the required number of labels. For instance, in a simple 2D navigation task, the success rate of the learned policies increases from 20% to 80% using just 20 visual labels, a 4-fold decrease in required human input compared to traditional reward learning methods. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. While it does preserve the properties of being compact, compactly generated, and having a compact topology, it does not preserve core-compactness. Moreover, this loss of properties is consistent with the intuition that the Smyth powerspace represents a way to interpret preferences in a weak and approximate manner, and preferences in such spaces are often not narrowly defined, which aligns with the nature of core-compact properties. Finally, we propose that the loss of core-compact properties in the Smyth powerspace may be attributed to the fact that core-compactness can be seen as a manifestation of preferences that are overly broad, which is in contrast to the preferences represented by the Smyth powerspace that are already weak and approximate, and therefore, cannot be effectively narrowed down to core-compactness. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration by significant margins on both absolute performance metrics and a relative detection efficiency metric, demonstrating the value of further research into density estimation techniques and a standardized test bed for out-of-distribution detection methods. Our implementation details are available online at https://github.com/aleksz/detect-oof. We propose a new metric, called Breach Score, which evaluates a method's ability to identify out-of-distribution data by measuring the percentage of background data that incorrectly triggers a detection signal. We found that density estimation performs better than model calibration in both absolute terms and when evaluated using Breach Score. While a limited range of techniques were initially considered, our analysis revealed the potential for significant improvements within this group and we present two innovative variants - K-Means Estimation and Transformance - that surpass the previous best results by substantial margins. Our methods achieve breach scores of 94.66% for K-Means Estimation and 95.35% for Transformance on the SuperGLUE dataset, significantly outperforming the prior best of 83.33%. We found that density estimation performances are particularly sensitive to the choice of background data which can lead to significant variations in breach scores. We discovered that background data sampled from long-tail distributions or obtained through data augmentation yield superior results when compared to data sampled from normal distributions or human-annotated backgrounds. We found that density estimation performances are particularly sensitive to model size, achieving higher breach scores with larger models despite increased overfitting. We found that early fine-tuning of pre-trained models yields better results and proposed data-driven approaches to determine the optimal fine-tuning data range based on density estimation performance. We found that background data obtained through Transformance yield Breach Scores up to 7% higher than other methods. In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract hard-to-determine microscopic properties and examine the influence of electric currents. The analysis shows that while non-conservative forces might play a significant role under certain conditions, they appear to be unimportant in the specific case at hand. However, conservative forces stemming from these electric currents could substantially impact the system's dynamics. The model's applicability to various driving mechanisms and motor geometries suggests its vast potential for applying to diverse systems. By combining our simulation approach with experimental adjustments, this analysis paves the way for accurately interpreting and driving innovations in nanoscale electric-coupled motors. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to $D$. By applying the $\oplus_f$ operation to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, element-wise, we can compute the $f$-Convolution of $g$ and $h$, which maps $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to $D$. A specific instance of $\oplus_f$ is the standard component-wise XOR operation, denoted as $\oplus_\mathrm{XOR}$. We propose an algorithm to efficiently compute the $\oplus_f$ convolution of two functions $g$ and $h$ over a domain $D$, which is significantly smaller than the brute-force approach for large enough $n$, with a time complexity of $|D|^{O(\log f(n))}$. Furthermore, our results can be applied to previously known concepts, such as the $\oplus_\mathrm{XOR}$ convolution, enabling us to obtain new and more efficient algorithms for it. These results can be further generalized and improved, leading to new outcomes. We study the category of finite domains $D$, which includes, but is not limited to, the domains $\mathbb{Z}_m$ for prime $m$ or $\mathbb{Z}_2^k$ for any $k$. Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel approach to generate synthetic human-like sketches, and evaluating the performance of different approaches. We observed that in the context of VR sketches, point-based methods excel in both human-drawn and synthetically generated sketches. We believe our work will serve as a starting point for future studies, and the associated resources will facilitate replication and advancement. The used data, code, and demos are publicly available at https://3d-vr-sketch.net/. Keywords: 3D retrieval, VR sketches, 3D shapes, sketch-based retrieval, online collection.

The effect of this relationship on the mass function is analyzed in terms of its consistency with the general relativity equations, and we find that when this relationship holds, it's usually difficult to get consistent solutions. The outcomes of this type of collapse are then explored, along with the effect of additional factors, such as pressure in a collapsing cloud. Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes. Additionally, we have employed this method to investigate the universal higher-order corrections to the entropy of black holes, including those spanning broad classes such as black strings and black holes possessing rotation and charge. This led to a discovery of the non-uniformity of higher-order corrections to the entropy of black holes in five space-time dimensions, revealing the corrections to be an intricate function of the cosine of the angle between the axis of rotation and the charge. We have also explored the applicability of our formalism to extremal double extremal black holes and identified a subset of solutions characterised by negative total electric charge. Lastly, we have successfully recalculated the leading higher-order correction to the entropy of the Kerr black hole and established that it adheres to the standard template, thereby substantiating prior findings. Moreover, we have discovered a non-trivial higher-order correction to the spin correction of the Kerr black hole. A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the upkeep of this simplified effect model with the policy's continuous updates. Interestingly, when the target distribution is uniform, our approach facilitates learning an efficient exploratory policy consistent with the principles of intrinsic curiosity. Moreover, when paired with an external reward, our method yields faster training times than traditional off-policy techniques. A thorough examination of our technique is presented within the context of a simple 2D locomotion task using the HuMano robot simulator. The research reveals that the integration of end-effect models and reward structures triggers a self-sustaining learning cycle, which triggers a rapid increase in robot success rates, surpassing the performance achieved through off-policy training. A notable aspect of this research is the emergence of an exploratory drive reminiscent of the intrinsic curiosity phenomenon, which arises when the target distribution is uniform.
