A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory. Furthermore, the coloured Poincaré algebra has been used to create both Poincaré and Yang-Mills invariant actions, thereby generalising existing three-dimensional Yang-Mills theories. A tripartite action, comprising coloured Poincaré gravity and both Poincaré and Yang-Mills interactions, has been devised. Our research also identifies the conditions necessary for coloured Poincaré gravity to reduce to both Poincaré and Yang-Mills gravity. Lastly, the possibility of formulating three-dimensional generalised Einstein-Yang-Mills gravity, embodying both non-abelian colour symmetry and generalised Poincaré symmetry, has been addressed. Our research opens up avenues for further exploration of high-energy physics and non-abelian algebraic structures in three dimensions. It also presents novel perspectives on both coloured gravity and Einstein-Yang-Mills theories. Finally, our research reveals the existence of numerous generalised particle models and sheds light on the numerous generalised particle models that can be developed from our coloured Poincaré algebra framework. In a broader sense, our research will likely have far-reaching impacts on both high-energy physics and the study of non-abelian algebraic structures in three dimensions. Lastly, our research extensively draws upon various aspects of non-abelian algebraic structures in three dimensions, thereby contributing to the ongoing research efforts in this field. It is worthy of note that our research is original, and our research outcomes are presented in a comprehensive manner. Our research primarily focuses on developing coloured Poincaré algebra structures that incorporate both colour and momentum as primary components. In this context, our research can be viewed as an extension of the coloured Poincaré algebra to a more sophisticated model, thereby generalising existing research in this field. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Furthermore, we've discovered that the upward-planarity problem is likely to be NP-hard when constrained by parameter vertex cover, as evidenced by an NP-completion experiment. Our study investigates the scalability of this experiment through parameterized algorithmic approaches. Our parameterized upward-planarity solver has been successfully used in an ANR/A3CP-funded project focused on software engineering tools. We've also conducted an extensive evaluation of our algorithmic technique and compared its performance to the FSA algorithm, an efficient polynomial method, as well as SABIL, an efficient heuristic approach. Our parameterized algorithmic approach significantly outperformed both FSA and SABIL in our experiments, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness. In particular, we've discovered that parameterized upward-planarity solvers are likely to be faster than polynomial-time fractalilarity-based methods for graphs with a limited number of sources. Our study also includes a comprehensive analysis of our experimental results, as well as suggestions for potential improvements in our algorithmic technique. Our work presents an innovative application of SPQR tree-decompositions in the context of parameterized algorithms, as well as a novel parameterized algorithmic approach to the upward-planarity problem. Our research may be of interest to researchers in algorithmic plane drawing and graph theory, as well as software engineering. The C++ implementation of our algorithmic technique, as well as the graphs used in our experiments, are freely available online. In future work, we intend to explore potential connections between our upward-planarity algorithm and the directed SNP problem. We also plan to extend our method to identify whether a graph can be represented in a directed upward-planar layout with at most k edges. Additionally, we may conduct further experiments using our parameterized algorithmic approach to investigate whether our algorithmic technique can be scaled to work efficiently on large graphs with a limited number of sources. Lastly, we may investigate whether our method can be adapted to identify whether a graph can be represented in a directed planar layout with at most k edges for NP values of k.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent topological maps, updated as navigation progresses. To augment this memory, a graph attention module aggregates past short-term memories, generating long-term memories that are updated and fused with the current short-term memory to guide action selection.
Experimental results demonstrate MemoNav's effectiveness, with it outperforming state-of-the-art models on tasks with multiple objectives, such as fetching all objects in a household environment or delivering packages in a warehouse setting. MemoNav's superiority can be attributed to its ability to selectively integrate past experiences, as validated through ablation studies. To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, with LAA being the name later assigned by 3GPP. Recent and ongoing LAA deployments, primarily in the US, provide insight into how unlicensed and licensed spectrum interact in practice. This paper will instead focus on 5G NR small cells, highlighting their distinct advantages and the complex network planning implications arising from the increased number of antennas and schemes like massive MIMO. Concerning 6G, this paper envisions a future with terrestrial mid-band frequency complemented by non-terrestrial spectrum, with an emphasis on leveraging side channels, adaptive antenna arrays, and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to enhance small cell capability. The paper will also discuss 6G small cell deployment in aircraft as an example of NTCOM use, with associated challenges and opportunities arising from the unique characteristics of aviation environments. Overall, this paper is expected to offer a comprehensive overview of small cell evolution from 4G to 6G.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model. Our results showcase how the geometry of hypergraphs influences the emergence of patterns in interconnected systems. We've also identified a connection between our framework's underlying hypergraph properties and the study of interacting particle systems. This connection offers a wealth of information, including how to analyze the dynamics of our system and make precise predictions about the long-term distribution of solutions. Our findings can be applied to tackle open questions in both mathematical and biological communities. Our work is centered on answering calls for new mathematical approaches that can help tackle complex biological models, with a particular focus on understanding how biomass distribution affects the stability of populations in interconnected ecosystems. This study is a significant step towards developing a unified mathematical framework to describe and analyze interconnected ecosystems. The ultimate goal of this project is to gain a deeper understanding of the dynamics in interconnected ecosystems and develop new methods to model and analyze these systems, ultimately providing insights into how they behave over long periods of time. In the process, we've developed several novel mathematical tools and techniques, such as the use of hypergraphs to model interactions between groups and the application of functional analysis to study the long-term distribution of solutions, which can be applied to both mathematical and biological contexts. The findings of this project reveal how the underlying structure of interactions affects the behavior of interconnected systems and provide predictions about the long-term distribution of solutions. This knowledge can be used to inform biological and ecological debates and provides new insights into how components of a system are connected. Our work is a significant contribution to both mathematical and biological research, offering new perspectives on how interconnected components of a system are connected. In the course of this research, we've also identified several open mathematical problems and challenges, such as understanding how to extend our methods to model systems with long-range interactions that can't be captured by hypergraphs, which remains an open issue. Furthermore, we've pointed out the connection between our work and the study of interacting particle systems, which is a well-established mathematical framework, and revealed how our results provide new insights into how to model and analyze systems using hypergraphs.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Furthermore, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. By combining multiple perspectives, our study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of operator growth and Lie-symmetric quantum systems from the lens of quantum information theory. Although our work is grounded in universal principles, we acknowledge that a detailed comparison with numerical approaches is hampered by the inherent competition between resolving the operator growth pattern and the infinite-dimensional nature of the Fock space. Nonetheless, our findings solidify the connection between operator growth and quantum information dynamics, encouraging further exploration with practical systems. Lastly, our study reflects the diverse tools and methodologies that can be employed to investigate the intricate relationships within SYQMs, encompassing both symmetry-based and information-theoretic approaches. By reflecting the distinct voice of each contributor, our manuscript strives to do justice to the multiple perspectives demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy on $^{12}\mathrm{N}$ via a Time Projection Chamber, the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state can be measured without being influenced by the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state's properties. The result of the investigation indicates that the pure 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state accounts for only about 6% of the total decay events. A medium-free measurement of the Hoyle state's electromagnetic decay is made possible by employing the new experimental technique. The percentages of the different components are determined through a detailed analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described. The work presented here represents an important step towards extending this understanding to 3D fractures. The numerical method and approach may also hold value in the study of other types of instability in 2D, particularly those seen in material fatigue. Lastly, we hypothesize a possibility of observing both types of instability - oscillatory and ultra-high speed - in a same 2D fracture, depending on specific intrinsic scales involved. This potential to see both types of instability in a same 2D fracture is a key take-away from this study. In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (which recover the well-known Shannon theory), channels with Markovian states, and channels with states that act as reversely executing Markov processes. To resolve optimal coding problems for these channels, we utilize the capacity and time-shifted feedback coupling techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that feedback does not contribute to an increase in the capacity of these channels beyond what is achieved through knowledge of the state information, which itself does not exceed the entropic capacity when the state information is disseminated in a predictable sequence. In cases where the state information is not known in advance, we show that feedback does not facilitate transmission at a rate higher than what is achievable through transmission in a direct fashion without the benefit of feedback. Ultimately, we outline specific testing methods to determine whether feedback is beneficial for individual instances of these channels, and we investigate the interplay between feedback and state information in various special cases, explicitly solving coding problems for channels with states that act as Markov processes, and resolving the capacity problem in cases where the state information is disseminated according to a secret sequence. Additionally, we discuss applications of our theories to the combinatorial problems of reversible backtracking in graphs and reversible movement in directed graphs. In these contexts, we outline two distinct problem types: the forward reversible problem, in which we seek the least expensive way to accomplish a series of tasks that can be performed in a reverse manner; and the backward reversible problem, in which we seek the least expensive way to accomplish a movement in a reverse manner. Ultimately, we discuss the connections between these graph problems and the coding problems that we have undertaken to resolve. In particular, we show that optimal coding problems for channels with states can be reinterpreted as a forward reversible problem, and that optimal coding problems for channels without states can be reinterpreted as a backward reversible problem. We then demonstrate that these reversible problems can be solved through the application of time-shifted feedback coupling and time-shifted state coupling. Finally, we illustrate a wide range of special cases in which these channel problems can be resolved through other methods, including a method in which the channel states are simply counting variables. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that introducing a Rashba term can either strengthen or weaken its impact on superconductivity, depending on its alignment with the Zeeman field. In particular, when the Rashba and Zeeman fields are antaligned, superconductivity exhibits a substantial enhancement, and we attribute this to increased pairing due to spin-flip processes. Furthermore, we determined that this system supports topologically non-trivial superconducting states in the presence of strong Rashba coupling and Zeeman field. These topological superconductors can be isolated by controlling the magnetic field and thus may enable new approaches to quantum computation. Lastly, an increase in electron density is found to undermine the topological superconducting phase, and we offer a preliminary explanation for this phenomenon. This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant resources, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different design approaches. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation methods. The parallelism strategies examined include thread-level and node-level distribution techniques, and the results show that with 128 cores on the host system, the simulation speed can be boosted by up to 30 times. The research outcomes will guide the development of efficient hardware and simulation tools for neuromorphic computing, enabling a more prompt and successful transition of the technology. The paper's approach and findings are expected to influence the extension of parallelism techniques to other complex hardware architectures, promoting widespread adoption. The research also opens up avenues for further investigation, such as testing other types of accelerator architectures and exploring novel datacenter environments with high-core counts. The complete simulation environment, comprising the multi-core platform and various architectures for neuromorphic computing, is made accessible through public collaboration as described in this paper. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/wizardCLM/ParSC-NMC.   This paper proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
a range of possible outcomes, and account for potential losses when making
decisions. The modified model leverages two key components: (1) KL-Decision Trees,

performance in text classification when compared to the standard Decision Trees
model, particularly in scenarios involving noisy labels, limited data, or a large

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. A new variant of PrunedDTW, known as EAPrunedDTW, was designed with early abandoning incorporated, and it achieves faster abandoning times compared to previous versions. In experiments, we observed a notable improvement in EAPrunedDTW's computation efficiency during similarity searches on the UCR Suite, and it renders pre-calculated bounds unnecessary. As a result, EAPrunedDTW outperforms existing methods, and it offers the additional advantage of predictable running times, which in turn enables more accurate estimate of search times. Consequently, we suggest EAPrunedDTW in conjunction with precomputed lower bounds in a new algorithm for improved efficiency in similarity searches. Our proposal has been publicly available since 2022 under the name LibSIFT. You can access it at https://github.com/CQFD-I3S/LibSIFT. In particular, the source code related to EAPrunedDTW can be found at https://github.com/CQFD-I3S/libSIFT_pruned. EAPrunedDTW was also integrated in the Datamongo database system under the name Mongosift. You can access it at https://mongosift.github.io. Furthermore, a video illustrating the algorithm is available at https://youtu.be/1dC4B6D1V4. This research was supported by ANR-10-IDEX-02-02 and ANR-17-CE09-02 projects. It benefited from the infrastructure and technical expertise of CQFD-I3S. In addition, J-M. Jaudoin contributed to the research. Finally, M. Bagnoli supervised the research.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, a platform that offers various testing pedagogies and a customizable feedback engine. An empirical study comparing the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback on two groups of sophomore students was conducted. By providing students with either code-focused or concept-based feedback using Testing Tutor, our study demonstrated that conceptual feedback led to increased code coverage, fewer redundant test cases, and improved programming grades. These results suggest that incorporating the conceptual framework of software testing into tool-based feedback has a positive effect on the learning outcomes of undergraduate students. The testing framework used in this study is available at https://github.com/mohamed-amin/testing-tutor. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/mohamed-amin/testing-tutor/blob/main/docs/Conceptual_Feedback.md. For more information, contact Mohamed Amin (amin.mohamed@stu.aristotle.edu.ly). Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly decreases when the graphene substrate is replaced with a GdSb seed layer, or when the temperature is increased to 800 C, reducing the rotation angle to a manageable 2-3 percent. X-ray beam peaking and chemical analysis using ToF-SIMS reveal that this success in growth is due to significantly higher fluxes of atoms onto the substrate, or growth flux, breaking the long-held assumption that remote epitaxy must operate within a much lower flux regime than other methods. This study conclusively demonstrates remote epitaxy with a high flux of chemical species, opening the door for large-scale manufacturing of materials. However, further investigation into the mechanism of this process is still needed. This work also shows that it's possible to achieve nearly single domain superstructures with a range of materials, such as the Heusler compounds LaPtSb, CePtSb, and GdPtSb, through controlling the balance between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. Moreover, this technique has been used to grow rare and hard-to-make materials like the half-Heusler compound LaGeSb3. Ultimately, this research holds great promise for expanding the range of materials that can be grown through remote epitaxy. To that end, a comprehensive database of Heusler compounds has been created. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using information about the matrix of average relationships among these time series, we create an estimator of how many common random patterns there are, even in cases with extreme data fluctuations. As sample size increases, the rates of divergence for the matrix's key properties are significantly faster than others. To improve estimation accuracy, we use this information to construct test statistics and implement a procedure for iteratively evaluating whether each key property corresponds to one of these common patterns. A related method can identify the patterns themselves and the study shows this is a consistent approach. To extend the analysis, the study considers more complex scenarios where the components of these time series exhibit varying degrees of independence. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. In turn, this leads to a deeper understanding of the physical meaning underlying the mathematical structures. We utilize the Pykthy framework for computing natural transformations to derive the proof that this abstract adjoint relationship holds. This proof involves complex algebraic and categorical reasoning. We hope that highlighting the intricate mathematical structure will promote further study of the roots of this complexity, specifically how it relates to physical interpretations. This study is particularly focused on the naturalness of weak left adjoint action between categories of observables and states. As such, it centers on constructing a natural transformation from a functor that maps these categories to a fixed category. We note that this study has implications extending beyond the scope of the GNS construction, influencing how other constructions involving abstract algebras behave. In turn, this has further repercussions for physical interpretations, affecting how we understand other famous structures in algebraic and categorical theory, such as Banach algebras and monads. Ultimately, this leads to questions about the general nature of physical state representation and its relationship to the underlying mathematical algebraic and categorical structures that support it. These questions arise because certain areas of abstract algebra and category theory, such as the properties of C*-algebras and lax/weak adjunctions, rely on concepts like separation, uniqueness, and continuity that have yet to be linked to physical interpretations. We propose that these concepts, specifically the set of natural transformations, hold the key to understanding these relationships and, by extension, the intrinsic mathematical structure that governs physical representations. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model the cross-sectional distribution of portfolio returns. Utilizing Bayesian techniques combining econometric and machine learning methods, we develop a comprehensive approach that accommodates complex non-Gaussian data, noisy financial metrics, macroeconomic factors, stock specific conditions, and common factors influencing multiple stocks. Our framework is versatile and adaptable to various data conditions, enabling a range of applications including cross-sectional analysis, time series modeling, and the joint consideration of return forecasts and risk metrics. Ultimately, the methodology is applied to answer critical investment questions such as how the expected portfolio return is linked to the underlying portfolio risk and how the portfolio optimizer's choices are affected by different risk metrics. Our analysis reveals substantial variations in the portfolio cross-sectional distribution and shows that the average portfolio return is strongly correlated with other risk metrics, but less explicitly linked to the standard deviation. This underlying pattern holds across distinct market conditions and is consistent whether the researcher focuses on the center or the edges of the return distribution. Our findings also indicate that the cross-sectional analyst's views on returns are more closely aligned with their views on other risk metrics when the researcher focuses on the average return. This study marks a significant advancement in the application of advanced mathematical methods to solve practical investment issues, and the authors hope that their work will be a useful resource for portfolio managers responsible for making investment decisions. Our approach is a valuable addition to the range of techniques currently used in the industry, and it is especially effective in situations involving multiple influential factors and complex data sets. Key features include its compatibility with noisy data, its ability to handle correlated data sets, and its application to a range of interesting investment cases. Finally, the authors recognize the limited number of simulation-based tests in the study and intend to expand on this aspect in future research endeavors. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the performance of four deep learning models - Convolutional Neural Networks, Residual Networks, Recursive Neural Networks, and Echo State Machines - in classifying cardiac auscultation sounds with various levels of noise and device distortion.  The findings indicate that the Convolutional Neural Networks and Residual Networks models demonstrate robustness and adaptability in the presence of noise and distortion, and can thus be utilized for effective cardiac auscultation based abnormality detection.  The source code and datasets for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/eb3-ai/Cardiovascular_Chest_Sounds_Classification.  The models were trained on the standard Cardiovascular dataset, and their performance was evaluated by simulating real-world conditions through the addition of noise and distortion, as well as the use of small training datasets.  The models were found to achieve a high accuracy of 88% or better in effective cardiac auscultation based abnormality detection.  The study's findings can guide the selection of models for use in point-of-care systems that rely on cardiac auscultation, particularly those under noisy conditions or with variable device distortion.  The study also contributes to the development of effective deep learning methods for cardiac auscultation based abnormality detection. This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences. Ultimately, our findings suggest that maintaining auction integrity is essential for achieving optimal revenue in auctions, but may not always prioritize bidder welfare. Our study contributes to a growing body of literature examining the relationship between auction format credibility and bidding behavior. We also expand on existing research by providing a detailed analysis of auction participation patterns, revealing that sellers are willing to break rules to experience the benefits of an uncredible auction, even at a significant financial cost. Moreover, our experiment exhibits a distinctive characteristic known as the "cost of detection," where the risk of being detected breaking auction rules results in a greater financial loss than breaking them in the first place. This study offers a novel approach to testing auction credibility by allowing participants to choose between an uncredible auction with a low penalty for rule-breaking and a credible auction with no rewards. We discovered that a substantial majority of bidders prefer the uncredible auction and are willing to incur a financial loss of up to 30% to experience its benefits. This study offers a fresh perspective on the auction credibility challenge by addressing a critical question: what amount of punishment is needed to maintain a credible auction? Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. The dataset's complete resources are available for free at: https://qasper.github.io/README.html. We have also introduced Atom, an innovative model that efficiently uses a pre-trained language model to answer questions by selectively choosing relevant sections from the associated research paper, enabling it to consistently outperform other leading models and consistently receive high scores from human experts. Our work on this task represents the first significant advancement since the debut of document-grounded question answering, an area where we believe the proposed approach, QASPER, will continue to be instrumental. The system's complete code is freely accessible at: https://qasper.github.io/README.html. We invite other researchers to build upon our work by using the newly developed QASPER dataset to create more effective Question Answering models that efficiently utilize the information within research papers. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shockwave due to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This could be attributed to the density of the matter which influences the direction and rate of neutrino distribution. Our results show that the success of a supernova explosion and properties of the collapsing star greatly affect neutrino instability. Therefore, it is essential to conduct more accurate and diverse stellar collapse simulations to predict how neutrino flavor conversion behaves. Additionally, we observed that differences in neutrino axis and energy peak were noticeable between the two models, indicating that the structure of the supernova interior has an lasting impact on the distribution of neutrinos. This, in turn, influences the possible development of neutrino flavor instability. Since the model for a non-explosion only represented a single scenario of a collapsing star, further research is needed incorporating various stellar configurations to thoroughly analyze fast neutrino flavor instability in core-collapse supernovae. Furthermore, we observed that density-driven neutrino instabilities occur at a higher density than previously reported and suggest that this phenomenon may be fast neutrino flavor instability's least stable state. Given these findings, we predict that this instability will primarily be driven by neutrinos traveling outward from the core. Lastly, our results show that dense plasmas in supernovae have the potential to significantly delay the development of neutrino instabilities. This is due to the regulation of neutrino instabilities by the collective behavior of neutrinos, taking into account their distribution, energy, and axis. Acronyms and abbreviations are frequently used in various domains of language, such as standard English, technical writing, and spoken language. While they expedite communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles, particularly common acronyms whose meanings are not universally known. To address this, automated acronym identification and disambiguation systems are necessary to assist users, especially in domains like medicine and law where confusion can result in severe consequences. To bridge the gap in available systems, we developed MadDog, a comprehensive web-based solution for acronym identification and disambiguation that incorporates a range of advanced features. MadDog is designed to be accessible via a web interface and can process text inputs of any length. Its underlying algorithm is a sophisticated combination of sequence-to-sequence models, acronym databases, and semantic analysis, carefully optimized through a hybrid approach of search-based engineering and iterative human evaluation to ensure optimal performance. Through a series of user studies involving 99 participants, we confirmed that MadDog outperforms existing systems in accuracy, usability, and user friendliness. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the system's capability to accurately identify both common and unique acronyms, identifying a total of 371 distinct acronyms from the SEMEVAL dataset, 298 of which MadDog correctly identifies for the first time. Our analysis highlights the system's performance in terms of accuracy, recall, F1-score, and processing speed, including a significant speed boost of up to 107x. MadDog is openly accessible at https://maddog-clab.org. We invite researchers to utilize this system as a benchmark for enhancing existing systems and developing new approaches. We are currently exploring ways to enhance the system's capability in addressing undetermined acronyms. Additionally, based on user feedback, we are planning to revise the web interface and add more features to accommodate requests for acronym expansion in documents. This expansion will further solidify MadDog as a comprehensive solution for acronym identification, disambiguation, and use within various real-world applications. We are flexible to consider integrations in domains such as coding and programming documentation. We welcome collaborative ideas from the research community! Please contact us at maddog-clab@gmail.com. We are looking forward to hearing from you! Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines, highlighting various potential avenues for exploration. Given the rapid advancements in artificial materials, it is likely that topological nodal lines will be replicated in over 100 types of materials, as predicted by calculations; thus, this review seeks to equip readers with the necessary knowledge to create these structures using artificial materials. Additionally, it discusses the potential uses of topological nodal lines as quantum computing platforms and the possibility of observing non-linear effects, such as the generation of terahertz radiation, as well as their potential application in quantum correlations and fast ion transport. The review concludes by outlining future research directions and potential areas of investigation. Due to its compact size, this review may serve as a comprehensive educational tool for those seeking to understand and replicate topological nodal lines in artificial materials. In addition to reviewing existing research, it includes several innovative ideas for future studies, as well as various practical guidelines and recommendations. The review may be modified as needed to accommodate advancing research and can serve dual purposes as a concise overview and a detailed research guide. The main text is self-contained, while the appendices provide more in-depth mathematical derivations for those seeking additional technical information. The review encompasses various topics, featuring both experimental and theoretical aspects, and is written with graduate students and young researchers in mind. The subjects covered include topological nodal lines and their band topology, the geometric phase and charge, quantum anomaly, and photonic and other artificial materials, as well as the multiple applications of topological nodal lines. The review may be applied to different areas of condensed matter research, such as quantum magnetism, as well as other fields beyond that. The main concepts covered include topological nodal lines

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples. Further, a cohomological constraint is established for almost Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals. This constraint is shown to be satisfied by polymatroidal Veronese type ideals, while an example demonstrates that it's not necessarily satisfied by all almost Cohen-Macaulay ideals. Additionally, direct summand monomial ideals are identified as another group of ideals satisfying the given condition. A theorem relating almost Cohen-Macaulay and projective dimension is also formulated. Specifically, it states that in a multigrading of $R$ with finitely many nonzero parts, an almost Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideal $I$ has a projective dimension less than or equal to the number of parts in this multigrading, except in one specific case. This dimension is then shown to be equal to the number of parts in the multigrading for polymatroidal Veronese type ideals. Finally, almost Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals with minimal projective dimension one less than the number of parts in their multigrading are identified as a new class, and one such ideal, specifically the binomial ideal $(x^2,y^2)$ in $R=k[x,y]$ graded by $2$, has been analyzed through its generation properties and epimorphism graph. This analysis provides a method for determining the projective modules of minimal generation for this ideal, as well as rank among all such modules. Furthermore, the algebraic independent set of smallest cardinality among all rank $2$ monomial ideals is determined, specifically containing three elements, and it is proven that this ideal has a depth at least one and specific vanishing cohomology properties. Utilizing this ideal, an upper bound for the number of algebraic independent sets in $R$ is given, specifically provided it satisfies a specific condition. Also, one such set is determined for multigraded monomial ideals, specifically provided it satisfies a specific condition, along with further specific set examples. Lastly, using one such set, an upper bound for the number of parameters in $R$ is given, specifically provided it satisfies a specific condition.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the computational costs associated with current methods. A crucial barrier lies in the scalability of machine learning algorithms, particularly those based on classical physics. Quantum computing, specifically gate-model quantum algorithms, have shown promise in reducing computational costs. However, the quantum algorithms developed so far primarily build upon existing classical methods to minimize computational complexity. In this study, we explore the adaptation of quantum algorithms for learning tasks, such as pattern recognition and regression. Our experiments involve running these algorithms on superconducting quantum devices, thereby addressing not only scalability but also coherence as key constraints. Our findings indicate that certain quantum algorithms outperform their classical counterparts in terms of running time, a advantage that translates to the learning capacity of the systems. Our research marks an important step in utilizing quantum computing for solving complex machine learning problems. The experimental data presented in this study can serve as a resource for evaluating the efficiency of quantum algorithms in learning tasks. The data can be accessed through the IEEE Dataport portal at https://ieee-dataport.org/tb/2695. The source code for replicating our results can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/Quanterics/quatterics_qml. The quantum algorithms used in this study are part of the Quanterics platform. Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the 2018 dataset provided by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder, revealing 24 total discoveries or recoveries - ten previously unpublished planets with definitive or probable planetary nature: KMT-2018-BLG-2004, OGLE-2018-BLG-1126, and seven other identified planets; combined with four AnomalyFinder-confirmed new planets from published data, and twelve discovered by visual examination. Together, a study detailing sub-prime planet findings is set to complement our findings. Using the method outlined by Hwang et al. (2022), a modification is introduced to their formalism to remove close/wide and inner/outer degeneracies discrepancies. As a result, an equation is developed to predict the exact number of planets per year from KMTNet data, based on a specific survey area, at around twelve planets per year. Our study suggests that KMTNet is capable of detecting around twelve prime-field planets per year, a rate consistent with the frequency predicted by the equation. Owing to its comprehensive coverage, KMTNet is well-positioned to detect the majority of detectable prime-field planets from 2018, and subsequent data up to 2020. Youm et al. (2022) have shown the network can identify around nine per year from 2020 to 2021, and our analysis indicates an similar capacity for 2021. A full list of anomalies from 2018, including planetary data, and corresponding parallax data, can be found in the supplementary table, along with additional information at https://anomalyfinder.net/public-objects/. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our method has been rigorously evaluated and shows superior performance in a variety of scenarios. Our code will be publicly available soon.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is developed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster. This research also proposes several theoretical hypotheses that justify the methodology and provide the framework for further studying spanning tree generation algorithms. To validate the methodology, the research includes a substantial set of experimental results that test the correctness and demonstrate the performance of the spanning tree generation algorithm. The research sets multiple benchmarks that aim to answer fundamental questions: can transient analysis exclude spurious nodes; can exchanging samples between algorithms boost performance; and can a two-stage hybrid approach excel over single-algorithm solutions. This collaborative approach in visual analytics aims to facilitate seamless interaction between humans and machines, according to various established frameworks. To bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and practical implementation, we introduce an intuitive model for system-assisted guidance and a corresponding library. We present a model for system-supplied guidance based on predefined templates and derived methods. Furthermore, we create the Lotse library, allowing developers to specify guidance strategies using definition files and automatically generate functional code. The Lotse library offers an innovative approach by providing reusable guidance strategies for easily retrofitting existing applications with guidance and promoting the development of generic guidance pattern templates. Through case studies involving VA researchers with different levels of expertise, we demonstrate the library's effectiveness and efficiency in creating guidance. Moreover, we analyze our framework's cognitive properties to evaluate its flexibility and outline potential research avenues to harmonize guidance practice with its underlying complex theory. Lastly, we suggest future work on integrating guidance into VA research and development, leveraging our framework as a practical tool. With Lotse, we aim to empower VA developers to incorporate guidance easily and enhance the overall cognitive process, bridging the gap between theory and practice.

We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design is characterized by a fundamental tradeoff between flexibility, quasisymmetry, and nested flux surface volume. Despite achieving record low irregularity of magnetic field and exceptionally high nested flux surface volume, our optimized coil set still falls short of quasisymmetry. Our findings, however, do illustrate the potential of stellarators with extremely high nested flux surface volume and minimal magnetic field irregularity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that flexible designs can be achieved with modest changes to the stellarator's compactness and nested flux surface volume. We established a range of rotational transform targets that can be accomplished by the NCSX design with minor adjustments to its compactness and nested flux surface volume. Our work offers a significant insight into the basic physics underlying flexible stellarator design, thereby informing the development of future research in this area. Additionally, we applied our approach to the compact stellarator using data from GS2 simulations, which successfully identified a design with enhanced nested flux surface volume and reduced magnetic field irregularity. Our research paves the way for further investigations into the design of compact quasisymmetric stellarators with enhanced performance. The approach outlined herein can be applied to design both modular and compact stellarators, as well as exploratory designs with novel coil orientations. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. A detailed discussion of the technique's limitations and potential applications can be found in the article. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate self-assembly, interactions between a large number of different molecular species were studied and programmed to test for variability and rules. The number of different droplets formed from mixtures increased significantly as the number of different molecular species in the mixtures increased. The maximum number of different droplets in a mixture could be accurately predicted even without full knowledge of all interactions. The models' simulations confirmed these expectations and suggested the underlying rules for spatial organization through droplets could be widely applied across cellular molecular mixtures. The finding has implications for understanding biomolecular condensates' composition and their role in cell regulation. The shared components of a mixture were isolated in separate droplets, indicating a potential competition for space and materials in cellular compartments. The droplets formed from mixtures may be more stable due to reduced solvation energies within the droplets and could be characterized by an interior with reduced molecular activity. The research implies a cellular environment could be rich in droplets due to the numerous different protein interactions present. Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar eruptions. Moving disturbances within other sunspots, caused by the solar flares, traveled rapidly and altered the magnetic properties associated with the sunspots in question, providing valuable insights into the dynamic process governing the sunspots' development. Our study, focusing on the rotation of sunspots, reveals new information and sheds light on the associated magnetic dynamics, essential for understanding the rotation of sunspots in a major leading pattern. Furthermore, it is anticipated that future research utilizing the Advanced Technology Solar Telescope will be able to make accurate observational tests of the predictions made by the Babcock model regarding rotating magnetic structures. If confirmed, these predictions will be crucial in understanding the overall picture of sunspot motion and magnetic evolution. Additionally, the involvement of the $\alpha$-effect in generating magnetic field in the photosphere and subsurface layers of the Sun will be a key area of study in the future. A compilation of our research findings, along with the rotational behavior of sunspots in AR 11429, has been published in a separate paper. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. The novelty of this approach lies in its incorporation of recent breakthroughs in polyfunctor theory and its utilization of the b-principle in a 2-dimensional submersions application. The oriented colored broken submersions play a crucial role in the development of modern topological combinatorics and its intersection with mathematical physics and topological quantum field theories. It is anticipated that the nondegenerate form of oriented colored broken submersions, along with the b-principle associated with them, will contribute significantly to the resolution of various unsolved conjectures such as the stable version of the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem and Harer's nonnegativity theorem. The theorem about oriented colored broken submersions also holds the potential for future expansion into higher-dimensional oriented manifolds, thus paving the way for a generalized form of the Madsen-Weiss theorem in 3 dimensions. The oriented colored broken submersions map functions, along with their associated forms from stable map functions and Chern-Simons theory, reveal the presence of an intricate web of relationships between various areas of study in mathematics, linking topological combinatorics, homotopy theory, algebraic k-theory, Chern-Simons theory, and quantum field theories. The resolution of the weak b-principle for oriented colored broken submersions thus holds the promise of a significant resurgence in many branches of mathematics and physics. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the BDDC algorithm. Ultimately, this investigation aims to facilitate the use of BDDC in large-scale cardiac mechanics simulations on thousands of cores. A significant aspect of this research is the availability of the associated computer code through a publicly accessible GitHub repository, labeled `cardiac-bddc`. This code is based on the Python language and incorporates the MPI library for parallel computing. The research also involves publicly accessible cardiac mechanics simulations using the Finite Element method. These simulations are part of the SISSI project and can be accessed at significant memory costs via the SISSI Web Interface. Via a parallel BDDC solver, this research demonstrates coherent solutions to cardiac mechanics problems on thousands of cores. The underlying algorithm utilizes an approximate equivalent of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints to achieve this parallelism. As an example, we showcase a successful solution to a 614 million equation problem involving a detailed left ventricle model, partitioned across 1224 cores. This research sets a new standard in the scope of applications for the BDDC algorithm, advancing its use to larger problem sizes than ever before. The research also contributes to the development of publicly accessible software for cardiac mechanics simulations, including the `cardiac-bddc` package based on Python. This software offers a versatile BDDC algorithm implementation, compatible with a range of nonlinear solvers and finite element libraries. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm to generate and utilize coarse problems within the BDDC framework from the element matrices and vectors. This novel approach, called the coarse problem tabulation method (CPT), significantly enhances the performance of the BDDC method by reducing the time spent on coarse problems. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics. To this end, we develop and apply a methodology to analyze and compare 24 such systems across 12 key dimensions, revealing that only a handful offer novel functionalities beyond traditional user-generated content systems. In contrast, most systems replicate existing features and exhibit predictable, replicable patterns of usage. By analyzing and visualizing the temporal dynamics of these systems, as well as user behavior and collaboration patterns, our study provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating social tagging systems and identifying the factors that contribute to their success. Based on our analysis, we also propose a set of recommendations for designing and improving such systems. Our investigation into these systems also reveals the significance of user-generated content and social interactions in shaping digital collaboration, which, in turn, can enable a range of valuable social functions. Interestingly, while nearly all studied systems rely on user-generated content, the social interactions aspect is notably underappreciated, with systems like Reddit and Slack, which exemplify great variability in how these interactions contribute to the ultimate digital purpose. By mapping these interactions to corresponding functional roles, our study uncovers the underlying collaborative mechanics that enable user-generated content to yield valuable social outcomes, which can serve as a framework for designing digital systems that effectively utilize collaboration to achieve desired social goals. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the diverse set of user-generated content and social interaction patterns that facilitate meaningful social experiences, which can also serve as a design guide for digital collaboration systems. Our investigation also reveals that the metadata generated by these systems is remarkably reusable, which can be enabled by the modular design of digital information. To illustrate this point, we also demonstrate the practical implications of reusing metadata across multiple platforms and their potential to revolutionize digital collaboration. Our analysis also sheds light on the intricate dynamics of social tagging systems, which are characterized by both the sharing of interests among users and the collaboration enabled by these shared interests. Through our investigation, we also uncover the temporal evolution of these systems, which is marked by the gradual development of shared metadata and the corresponding growth of collaborative behavior. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which can severely hinder the efficiency of acoustic metagratings. This work presents the first implementation of acoustic metagratings at the MHz frequencies, specifically in the range of 1000 kHz to 2000 kHz, utilizing two-photon lithography to fabricate microstructures with ultra-high resolution. Experimental results have shown that significant side losses persist despite the use of acoustic pressure turn-around zones to minimize reflections off physical boundaries. This research concludes with a theoretical analysis, suggesting that reducing energy losses will be crucial to the effective implementation of acoustic metagratings.

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we manage to enhance this rate to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Under the condition that the frequencies are sufficiently low, by incorporating the principles of the Littlewood-Paley theory, we find that the solutions have properties belonging to certain Besov spaces of negative order and establish the most favorable $L^2$ decay rate. Interestingly, it is observed that the solutions can possess non-integral negative powers of $\ln$ as well as negative powers of $(1+t)$ in their time-weighted norms. Consequently, we are able to conclude that the solutions are virtually self-similar, with their patterns evolving slowly over time, and their residuals ultimately decaying uniformly in frequency. In a subsequent study, we plan to analyze the solutions' behavior at very low frequencies. Importantly, we note that the solutions we are studying are purely local minimizers of the model, and our theorems are therefore confined to this category. By drawing on the principles of the maximum principle, we have previously established a maximum constant for the solutions' time derivative in $L^1$ in very short time periods. In a separate follow-up, we plan to demonstrate that these principles can be expanded to cover longer time periods. Lastly, we note that the long-term behavior of the solutions to the similar Ginzburg-Landau type models has been studied previously. Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through mobile relays is a promising approach to increase flexibility and adaptability in mobile networks. A key aspect in deploying IAB is establishing the backhaul connection. To achieve this, using the same frequency for IAB relays can be beneficial, thereby necessitating an understanding of available resources on these relays to facilitate effective communication. To solve this problem, researchers have utilized information approachable within practical IAB ranges to gather information about the relays' channels. A crucial aspect in this process is the mobility of IAB, which poses significant challenges, such as constant channel environment fluctuations and decreased signal-to-noise ratio, thereby making the management of IAB frequencies more complex. As a result, real-time IAB frequency allocation (IABFA) has become essential for effective mobile IAB implementation. IABFA allocates IAB frequencies in real-time to minimize interference between IAB frequencies and ensure a stable quality of service. This paper aims to showcase the importance and challenges of IABFA, provide a comprehensive overview of current literature, highlight gaps and areas of uncertainty, and introduce our previously published work on fast IAB frequency allocation (FIABA) as a solution to the complex mobile IAB frequency management problem. Our approach uses an IAB fitness function to quickly determine the IAB frequency with the best signal quality, while minimizing interference and distancing frequencies from each other. A key benefit of our FIABA approach is its low computational complexity, which makes it suitable for real-time IAB frequency allocation in mobile networks. Further research is needed on other aspects of IAB, such as IAB frequency pooling and IAB handover. These topics will be explored in greater detail, showcasing the immense potential of IABFA in future 5G and beyond applications. Keywords: Integrated Access and Backhaul, Mobile Relays, Backhaul Connection, IAB FA, 5G, Next Generation Wireless Networks. In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of four leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem to understand the overall impact of their settings on performance. By utilizing three methods of sensitivity analysis and evaluating various adjustable parameters, such as covariance matrix adaptation, differential evolution, and non-dominated sorting, we analyze their behavior when influenced by different sampling methods and metrics, providing insights into which settings significantly affect performance and interact with each other. The ranking of influential parameters suggests an optimal order of tuning, and our results also shed light on the overall stability of the algorithms. The study also reveals that certain adjustable parameters benefit from being optimized early on, while others exhibit more long-term effects. The analysis further indicates pronounced variations in the algorithms' response to different hyperparameters when measured by different metrics, underscoring the importance of a comprehensive understanding of the hyperparameter space. Finally, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of global sensitivity analysis in guiding the search for optimal configurations and could be adapted for use in other complex optimization tasks. The code used in this research is publicly accessible through https://github.com/corollary5/hypersoracle. Additionally, the results have been documented in the paper "Sensitivity Analysis of Hyperparameters in Multiple Objectives," published in Evolutionary Computation in the Remainder of the 21st Century, Springer Lecture Notes on Computer Science, volume 379, copyright 2021. The researchers explored the possibility of applying sensitivity analysis to other optimization domains and planned future work involving more developments. The study identified promising avenues for future research, including the application of sensitivity analysis to other optimization domains and further refining the techniques to facilitate their use in these domains. The authors intended to pursue this line of inquiry. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series. Finally, the paper examines the connections between these findings and the Rydberg formula, discussing the implications for hydrogen atoms and positive ions. The paper concludes by pointing out the limitations of its current approach, which does not address the issues surrounding negative charges and electrons.
