Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to learn and adapt when prerequisites about the tasks are unknown or if new information is introduced unexpectedly. In response to these challenges, the field of lifelong reinforcement learning has emerged, aimed at developing models capable of learning and adapting to diverse sets of tasks. To bridge the gap between theoretical frameworks and practical implementations, we introduce an extensive benchmark called L2Explorer, featuring a rich 3D navigation environment with an infinite number of learning situations that can be tailored to suit a variety of scenarios, including gradual task shifts and sudden changes. This benchmark is designed to test the ability of lifelong reinforcement learning models to learn, adapt, and generalize across a broad spectrum of assessment learning tasks. To validate its effectiveness, we compare several cutting-edge models to baseline models, demonstrating L2Explorer's value as a standardized tool for evaluating lifelong reinforcement learning methods. The benchmark's source code and training data are publicly available at https://github.com/AIUnion/l2explorer. L2Explorer can be accessed through our dedicated website: l2explorer.aiunion.com. L2Explorer is now an official benchmark recognized by the ACL community. Please see our submission guidelines at https://l2explorer.aiunion.com/benchmark_submission. L2Explorer aims to support the research community by providing standardized tools for evaluating lifelong reinforcement learning models and we look forward to collaborative efforts with the community in the future. Lastly, we present an approach, called Transfer Via Randomized Enumeration (Transfer-REN), which leverages the structure of related tasks in L2Explorer to efficiently transfer knowledge and achieve significant improvements over baseline models, surpassing existing state-of-the-art results. The code for Transfer-REN is publicly available at https://github.com/AIUnion/tvern.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory. This paper outlines the design and logic of the data processing system, the chosen interface architecture, and the planned communication interface with external software components. It also provides a brief presentation summary of the results and the proposed solution, aiming to facilitate collaboration and input from the scientific community before implementation begins. This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves is directly proportional to their distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where a damping mechanism prevents long-term perturbations. This research is particularly notable given that it contrasts with previous results showing no non-trivial travelling waves in areas immediately surrounding Couette flow with regularity higher than $3/2$. To achieve this discovery, we create a mathematical framework that enables us to control the vorticity of these waves while exploiting certain properties of Hamilton's equation, resulting in an effective dissipation rate of $\lesssim |\xi|^2$. This process is challenging due to the lack of a Biot-Savart operator's smoothing properties, which typically requires at least three-eighths regularity to operate effectively. This limitation is overcome by employing a novel approach that involves using the Biot-Savart operator in an integral form, thereby increasing the available 'gain' in the exponent and effectively compensating for its shortcomings. Consequently, we are able to derive an effective dissipation rate of $\lesssim \langle \xi^2 \rangle$ and establish a critical regularity threshold of $s=\frac{3}{2}$ for these travelling waves in the vorticity $H^s(\mathbb{R}^2)$. Moreover, by utilising several techniques such as integrating by parts, splitting the kinetic energy into relative and absolute components, and a few other well-known arguments, we are able to provide a sharp bound for these waves' dissipation rates and conclude that they cannot persist in non-weak solutions with regularity higher than $3/2$. Finally, through a combination of the inverse Biot-Savart operator and a modified version of the standard regularisation theory, we are able to show that these travelling waves can be eliminated in scenarios involving regular solutions with extra spatial smoothness. Notably, our study has broader implications, allowing us to control the growth of solution perturbations under certain conditions in areas beyond Couette flow. To achieve this, we can modify the aforementioned dissipation rate argument while exchanging the reference solution to any other smooth planar flow. This opens the door to future research on the existence and characteristics of these travelling waves

Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties. Additionally, this technique allows exploring the behavior of exciton-polariton condensates in complex environments. These findings have important implications for developing optical spin-based technologies and studying polarization condensates in intricate optical systems. The polarization control exhibited could be employed to create polarization-sensitive optical traps with various shapes, enabling the manipulation of exciton-polariton condensates in complex scenarios. These results offer a starting point for exploring exciton-polariton condensates in intricate setups and developing advanced optical technologies based on spin-photon interactions. The developed technique could be applied to create advanced all-optical devices, such as filters and rotators, utilizing spin-photon entanglement and allowing control of polarization with high precision. This study investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the p-Laplace equation with nonlocal growth conditions, coupled with a reaction term, subject to mixed boundary conditions. The reasoning employed builds upon previous work of the second author, adapting it to accommodate the more general Laplace equation with nonlocal growth conditions. The proof relies on a combination of functional analysis and the selection principle for 1-harmonic functions. The main challenge addressed is the absence of a maximum principle for the given equation, requiring an innovative approach. Furthermore, we extend existing literature by exploring the interaction of solutions to the given equation with k-harmonic functions. The proof involves establishing a relevant representation formula, followed by a combination of the selection principle and functional analytic techniques. Finally, we analyze the spatial behavior of solutions to the given equation, proving a maximum principle and establishing its relationship with 1-harmonic functions. The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical transmission details. Recognizing the need to effectively share this information, the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact research team developed an open-access data platform comprising a data warehouse and an online dashboard, enabling transparent and efficient data sharing. This endeavour revealed challenges pertaining to data availability, credibility, and governance in the public sphere within South Africa. This research aims to address these concerns by presenting the successful implementation of a public-facing data platform as a model solution to the existing data-related problems. The paper outlines our journey in constructing this platform from available data sources to the creation of an online dashboard, subsequently serving as a data-driven tool for the public and informative data-driven decision-making instruments for policymakers. This research will serve as a reference for institutions seeking to establish data platforms in the public sphere and as a prototype for making decisions supported by data in the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak in South Africa. The research is also notable for its adherence to the principles of responsible AI, specifically by addressing the ethical concerns surrounding data governance in the public sphere. The research provides a model that can be replicated for data-driven decision making during the pandemic and in the future, emphasizing the importance of data credibility, transparency, and accountability in making data-driven decisions. The research highlights the challenges of data-driven decision making during the pandemic, specifically the difficulties in acquiring reliable and credible data and maintaining data consistency, in addition to the accountability of data-driven actions. The research offers a data platform as a solution to these challenges, serving as a model for institutions to share data and make data-driven decisions in the public sphere, especially during the pandemic and in the future. The research will serve as a reference for institutions seeking to establish data platforms in the public sphere. In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more precise opinions. For retinal analysis in particular, recent advancements have led to increased use of multiple imaging methods: standard two-dimensional fundus photographs and more detailed three-dimensional imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography. Our study employed three distinct multimodal data fusion strategies centered on deep learning to tackle not one but two complex conditions: glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of fusing different medical data types to achieve better outcomes in retinal analysis. Our implementation details and code are available for others to build upon. Currently, these approaches are primarily theory-based but our evaluation is done through experiments rather than theory so that others can verify the efficacy in real-world scenarios. Our contributions include successfully combining information from two-dimensional and three-dimensional OCT images to achieve better outcomes and demonstrating that our approaches perform significantly better than existing state-of-the-art models. Our approaches have shown outstanding results with specific data sets by achieving accuracy rates of 97.66%, 97.13%, and 96.67% in our evaluation, which surpass the current best performance by a considerable margin. Our research has notable practical implications as well, including reducing errors associated with missing critical information in fundus photos and providing more precise diagnosis by leveraging the advanced insights provided by OCT and OCT angiography. Our outcomes suggest that multimodal information fusion not only offers theoretical benefits but also significant practical advantages, which should be further explored in future research. Our current limitation is that our data sets are relatively small so our models have been trained on data that is not available to the eye care professionals making the diagnosis, which raises concerns about generalizing the outcomes. Our future work will focus on addressing these challenges so that our approaches can be effectively applied in real-world diagnostic settings. Our initial findings suggest that our models can be improved even more by further training using data that is currently unused, which could lead to even more precise diagnoses. Our future work will also involve expanding our approaches so that they can be utilized for a broader range of diseases. Our ultimate goal is to develop diagnostic systems that can automatically detect a wide range of eye problems, which would significantly contribute to improving eye care. Our contributions will include reducing the need for unnecessary eye exams, providing essential information for insurance claims, and ensuring that patients are informed about their condition and the best course of treatment. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. While the focus of this study remains on extracting features to study severe symptoms, it is hypothesized that similar lung abnormalities may contribute to other critical COVID-19 symptoms, such as myocarditis and neurological disorders. As such, it is suggested that this technique may also be applied to study these other critical symptoms. It is expected that the features extracted from X-ray images will contribute significantly to developing other important COVID-19 symptom classification tasks. In the future, it is anticipated that deep learning models trained on large, well-annotated datasets will surpass the current approach in performance. Nonetheless, it is conjectured that the economic and practical value of leveraging X-ray images will persist as a valuable tool for detecting high-risk patients. To this end, it is envisioned that lung imaging will continue to play a pivotal role in directing limited medical resources towards patients requiring critical care during the pandemic and beyond. As such, it is predicted that lung imaging will remain a crucial component of pandemic decision-making. We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interactions and a new dataset for object-object relationships. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the maximum L1 norm of the multiplier, and can be calculated efficiently for any number of bits. Our improved model allows us to achieve better results in a shorter time compared to the current best techniques, with significant gains for certain configurations. For example, a certain MCM operation can be performed with fewer than 180 one-bit adders, whereas the previous techniques required at least 184 adders. Our work also introduces a novel hardware cost model that can be easily adapted for MCM operations over finite Gaussian fields and shows promising results in this domain as well. Our techniques are now available in an open-source tool that can be used for generating C or HDL code. Our work demonstrates that the ILP model, combined with an efficient tool, can efficiently generate multiplierless circuits with optimal adder counts, surpassing the current best techniques in several cases. Our novel hardware cost model is more accurate, additive, and efficient, and can be easily adapted to new complex MCM operations, making it a more effective tool. Our experiments reveal that our approach can also be successful in circuits with non-optimal hardware cost, and even outperform the current best techniques in some cases. Our work presents several interesting research questions that we plan to investigate in our future research. Firstly, we need to resolve the time complexity issue by developing more efficient algorithms. Secondly, we need to establish the adder complexity as a sufficient condition for optimal MCM operations. Lastly, we need to explore new applications of MCM operations, such as in neural networks and other domains. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM operations and opens new avenues for its use in other domains, making it a valuable contribution. \paragraph{Abstract} This paper presents a novel approach to performing Multiple Constant Multiplications (MCMs) with minimal hardware costs. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further research by Khuller, Peleg, and Trevisan developed a PTAS for several graph classes including $k$-tree graphs, for which the PTAS does not directly apply.

We present a new PTAS for solving general-valued CSPs with a specific property. The class of graph families for which this PTAS is achieved includes those with restricted tree-like structure, such as $k$-tree, Bollob\'{a}s-Riainetti graph, and $k$-outerplanar graphs.

The PTAS relies on a promising yet previously unrecognized approach, involving approximate solution forecasting. We show that restricting input values to a specific range allows the PTAS to utilize an efficient scheme, achieving an $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\log m)$ approximation, where $m$ is the number of variables. On certain graph classes, such as $k$-tree, this leads to better results than previously known algorithms. The research also presents a more efficient version of the Baker PTAS for Maximum Independent Set, reaching an $O(\frac{\log m}{\sqrt m}$ approximation. Finally, we derive new PTAS for minimum vertex cover, and, as a byproduct, for other complementary problems, such as maximum matching and independent set with specific constraints. The research uses new tools for approximate solution forecasting and a concept we call approximate solution consistency. We also introduce several techniques to efficiently apply these ideas to achieve PTAS on various graph classes. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected anomalies are not due to any underlying uncertainties, and ruled out detection errors. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after a linear-time preprocessing delay. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. The success of this foundation will be built upon demonstrating that a RAM with only basic addition operations can perform essential arithmetic operations efficiently after a constant delay, and using this foundation, we demonstrate key linear-time computability results for problems like Exact-Sums, Peano Arithmetic, and Clique, proving that these problems can be computed in linear time on a RAM with basic addition operations. Furthermore, this research will be achieved without invoking any non-standard arithmetic operations or using an explicit stack to facilitate computation. The paper also expands the existing theory of RAM classes to include a broader range of computation models, including multi-HEAD RAM systems, which exhibit intriguing counterexamples and highlight the complexity of establishing $NTIME[lin] \neq LINDCM-1TIME[lin]$ under certain additional constraints. A RAM with a two-head operation capability computed $F_2$-gate evaluations, but a single-head operation computed the same task only after a linear delay, and another result shows that even with multi-head operations, certain problems like Exact-Sums and Peano Arithmetic require linear-time computation. Finally, this research presents general criteria under which a monotone $F_2$-gate evaluation can be computed in linear time on a single-head RAM system. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object positions, orientations, and scales are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Notably, as training progressed, the essential parameters for transmitting useful information were identified within the RNN's recurrent connections, thereby justifying the utility of recurrence in object categorization tasks.  This study provides a systematic approach for diagnosing and interpreting the role of recurrence in various tasks.  Furthermore, our results suggest that object-related auxiliary variables are consistently exchanged across recurrent iterations, with positional information exhibiting particularly high variability across recurrent iterations.  Ultimately, this work offers a crucial insight into how RNNs function and highlights the significance of leveraging contextual auxiliary variables in object categorization, particularly in cluttered environments.  This research may have far-reaching implications for the design of future object categorization systems.  Code for the project is available at https://github.com/ashishkaramala/objcat_rnn. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. The Hatano-Nelson chain offers a versatile model system that can be used to experimentally verify the influence of correlations on non-Hermitian topological phenomena. The Hatano-Nelson chain is readily realizable in various platforms, including ultra-cold atoms and superconducting quantum wires. The properties of this system can be accurately measured using techniques such as Raman radar, tunneling spectroscopy, and X-ray spectroscopy by adjusting the chemical potential according to the number of particles in the system. The reduced point-gap topology in one dimension can also be observed in systems with two synthetic dimensions, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry, as demonstrated using a two-dimensional Majorana model. The reduction of the point-gap topology in one dimension is attributed to the emergence of a zero-mode edge that is present in both the geometric and non-geometric phases. The zero-mode edge is characterized by two unique properties: (i) a localized density distribution and (ii) a vanishing density at the edge. The discovery of this zero-mode edge underscores the non-trivial correlation-induced topological effect in one-dimensional systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. The reduced point-gap topology in one dimension is also associated with an invariant polynomial that is constructed using the Gau\ss\  integral, along with a set of specially designed fermionic operators that exploit the reducibility of the Hatano-Nelson chain. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few isolated instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. This research promises to provide further constructions in multi-dimensional spaces through the application of the Cayley graph and Ramanujan graphs. Keywords: Golay complementary arrays, multi-dimensional spaces, ring identities, omnidirectional precoding.

As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovations in both techniques and their practical applications. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently implementing and prototyping nature-inspired optimization algorithms. By integrating 15 established techniques and 112 benchmark functions, as well as supporting 11 novel hypercomplex-based approaches, our framework surpasses others in its domain, thus marking it as a groundbreaking innovation in optimization software development. Utilizing LibOPT under the C paradigm proves to be remarkably user-friendly and adaptable, as evidenced by the inclusion of source code examples demonstrating the practical usage of benchmark functions. This feature enables researchers to experiment with different approaches within a specific framework, ultimately facilitating their comparative evaluation. Through a comprehensive performance evaluation, we demonstrate the feasibility of using LibOPT on large-scale datasets, ultimately highlighting its capabilities as an effective tool for optimizing real-world engineering problems. As a substantial contribution to the optimization community, LibOPT's source code and additional supporting materials are freely accessible under an permissive license, thereby empowering researchers to further enhance the framework and utilize its features to address various problems. Furthermore, we investigate the practical usage of benchmark functions, revealing that many researchers still face challenges in properly evaluating their approaches, as shown by an analysis of recent publications in top-ranked journals. This analysis guides researchers on several key issues: comparing multiple algorithm evaluations, employing comprehensive function assessments, selecting optimal solution quality metrics, and incorporating human expertise in decision-making processes. By addressing these concerns, researchers can critically evaluate their experimental designs and enhance the validity of their future work. Additionally, we delve into the possibilities of combining optimization techniques and propose a novel approach, known as hybridization, utilizing both techniques, as evidenced by the successful integration of the global pattern search method and the particle swarm optimization algorithm. Last but not least, we investigate the practical application of optimization techniques in solving two real-world problems, thereby demonstrating their practical relevance and utility. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. Notably, a degree d variety is found to have an infinite transitivity degree if and only if it is defined by at most d linearly independent equations. This finding reveals that certain degrees are "infinite" despite being associated with a finite number of equations. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieved top-tier outcomes, securing first, second, and third place in both the misogyny identification and classification tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate the beneficial impact of cross-entailment tasks on the model's performance. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub, and we invite interested researchers to build upon our work.

Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation. Notably, our research focuses on the theoretical aspects of this approach and shows that imposing a confidence limit on the GP's predictions prevents the controller from drifting into off-limits states. Moreover, our studies reveal that this confidence limit also serves as an incentive for the controller to move towards areas with higher rewards, thus facilitating navigation towards target states. In practical terms, constraining the GP's uncertainty facilitates policy learning and contributes to a controller that can adapt to new situations quickly and effectively. In a series of simulations, our findings confirm that controllers with this approach can achieve higher success rates and reduce navigation time by as much as 40% in a challenging 10-dimensional scenario. In contrast, the conventional method of constraining the GP's width to prevent the controller from drifting into off-limits states proves less effective. In particular, this approach increases the likelihood of the controller becoming stuck in high-elevation areas during airball navigation and leads to lower rewards relative to the constrained uncertainty method. Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. Caching and computation schemes often share a common thread being a part of the broader class of schemes that are known as layered schemes. This paper examines the properties of layered schemes in the context of wireless networks, with a focus on schemes involving packets $\mathcal{N}$ and timeslots $\mathcal{T}$. It establishes a new framework for linear schemes with parameters $n$, $t$, and $\Delta$, based on matrices $\Delta$ and time-scheduled matrices $\Delta_t$. This new framework, called the $\Delta$-framework, defines new parameters such as width, rank, submatrices, and vectors, enabling a comprehensive study of the $\Delta$-framework. As an example of its utility, the paper uses the $\Delta$-framework to develop a new caching scheme with improved performance and new tradeoffs. It also shows that various known caching schemes are special cases of the $\Delta$-framework, with a new perspective offered on existing research. Further research is conducted on the properties of width, rank, submatrices, and vectors within specific cases such as trees and graphs. The paper demonstrates that various key network communication challenges can be expressed as layering problems, with the $\Delta$-framework providing a universal solution. A new approach is also presented for linear schemes with arbitrary parameters $n$ and $t$, based on width and rank properties. Finally, the paper shows that the new approach is flexible enough to cover various important cases such as caching and distributed computation. A new computation scheme is designed based on width and rank properties, with a new distance metric introduced that surpasses current state-of-the-art compression methods. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality. Furthermore, our formalization of the Scott model forms the basis for a more comprehensive development of domain theory within univalent type theory, as well as for other applications of the lifting monad. The full development has been formalized and is available in Coq under the name "lifting-pcf". The core contribution of this paper lies in adapting the lifting monad to facilitate a formalization of the Scott model, and we hope that this adaptation will yield other useful applications of the lifting monad within univalent type theory. The paper also offers additional information on potential uses of the lifting monad, as well as a detailed analysis of why some of these ideas may not have been successful in the context of extensional type theory. Lastly, the paper includes a discussion on the potential for further integration of domain theory with other areas of predicate univalent type theory, such as dependent pattern matching and Barthe's resource logic. The development of these areas and the lifting monad could likely be mutually beneficial. Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$. 
The resulting cancellations have been obtained by computing isomorphisms of space representations, specifically those generated by the combinations of two Speh representations, through the application of the Rallis-Asaoha map, allowing for generalisations to be made for any $s_1,s_2\in\mathbb{C}$. 
The representation isomorphisms were obtained using Rankin-Selberg Serre's relations, essentially demonstrating that certain Eisenstein series can be cancelled out. 
The application of the Rallis-Asaoha map has provided a new method in the field, allowing investigations into the cancellations of Eisenstein Series to be made within a specific space. 
The mappings obtained from the Rallis-Asaoha map have shown potential in the field, allowing for the representation isomorphisms to be described in a test function space, particularly Dirichlet L-Functions, which may offer further opportunities and applications. 
The work may offer further opportunities and directions for further research, especially in relation to degenerate Eisenstein Series, although specific applications and directions have not been included in this paper.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. The developed approach presents a significant advancement in developing practical and geometrically informed collision avoidance systems for complex robots. Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show a clear increase above a binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ fit, and their transverse momentum spectra follow a similar trend as Au$+$Au collisions, involving a similar number of participants. We have determined the inverse slopes of the photon excess spectra at $285\pm53$(stat)$\pm57$(syst) MeV/$c$ and $333\pm72$(stat)$\pm45$(syst) MeV/$c$ for minimum bias and most central events, respectively. Moreover, we found that the photon rapidity density in Cu$+$Cu demonstrates a similar power-law behavior versus charged particle multiplicity observed in Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy. We have explored various sources of activation to explain the observed phenomena, including semihadronic emission and thermalization of matter, and have determined their contributions. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather conditions and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish them.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather conditions.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. Our method demonstrates an above 90% accuracy rate for single-camera implementations, and its integration with a sensor network shows an significant improvement in accuracy when compared to a system using image data from a single camera. We have made the RFS dataset and our source code publicly available. Additionally, we have established an online challenge for weather classification, with a focus on testing the effectiveness of various deep learning models and other approaches. More information on this competition can be found at https://www.challenge.ai/c/weather-classification.

Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. We also discover that science journals and policymakers tend to follow changes in the economics field, while the general public's interest is influenced by perceptions from science journals, policymakers' actions, and economists' recommendations. Finally, our findings imply that targeting influential groups, such as scientists, economists and policymakers, could be a strategic approach to shaping public climate change discourse. Moreover, our research highlights the significance of considering the role of perceptions in modeling public interest, particularly in issues like climate change, where fact-based evidence is crucial. Along these lines, our study offers a methodological approach to creating a Climate Change Index that can be utilized in further analyses. Building on this idea, our analysis also explores how different climate change mitigation policies might impact the relative interests of various groups, employing a structural econometric analysis technique. Ultimately, our results suggest that policies successfully promoting sustainable economic growth are also crucial in fostering the general public's understanding of climate change science, thus potentially acting as a bridge between economic concepts and climate change-related social norms. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control requirements. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update and refine a dynamic model in real-time. By integrating the updated model into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) structure, our approach enables successful deployment on multi-fingered soft robotic grippers. Our results demonstrate a high success rate in grasping diverse objects, even those initially unknown to the controller, as compared to other model-extraction methods. Additionally, our approach has been validated through a series of experimental trials, as showcased in a publicly available video. This research represents the first application of the Koopman operator theory in tuning and updating dynamic models for controlling soft robots. Furthermore, our approach presents a novel robotic control paradigm that uses model-learning and online-learning approaches synergistically. This research has the potential to broaden the application of data-driven methods to infinite-dimensional non-linear systems, as seen in soft robotic control. All experimental data and software have been openly shared in accordance with this research's goals. These assets can be utilized by the robotic community as a benchmark for developing novel algorithms to control soft robots. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods. We demonstrate examples of successful applications to both machine learning and tensor network algorithms. Additionally, our approach offers insights into the underlying geometry of these problems, thereby revolutionizing the field of optimization. Our proposed method is called the Geometric Gradient Descent method. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients. Moreover, by carefully examining the model's behavior, this study derives key insights into the relative importance of different data modalities in survival time prediction. As such, this work presents a novel approach to multimodal learning in survival analysis and provides valuable insights into the decision-making process of healthcare professionals. The findings and model are made available to support the research community. Leveraging the strengths of both textual and visual data sources, this study opens the door for further optimization, improving the accuracy of survival time predictions in lung cancer patients based on diverse data modalities. Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. Our
work on role specification provides a framework for guiding other dialogue
system architectures and our open-source implementation enables other researchers
to replicate our findings by accessing our dataset creation and dialogue system
integration code. Lastly, a demo of our role-compliant chat system is available
online for public access. With this, we aim to stimulate further research into
the area of role-constrained open-domain dialogue. In particular, we pose the
question of whether a chat system should be considered natural if it successfully
meets a role requirement, thereby indicating that our work has addressed the
problem, or if more substantial achievements are needed from the viewpoint of

examination of the relationship between our role specification, the properties

To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our two-dimensional analytical model effectively considers the spatial interdependence of RSUs, vehicle relays, vehicle users, and road infrastructure using a Cox point process. By assuming relay backhaul to RSUs over reserved wireless channels and user association with the closest RSU or relay, we calculate the probability that a typical user is linked to either an RSU or a relay, determine the SIR coverage probability of a typical user, and subsequently, calculate the average transmitted data rate and coverage area of an typical user. This method enables the quantification of the influence of relays on users' coverage and the optimization of the network through the comparison of various scenarios. Our findings show that the use of vehicle relays significantly enhances the network's performance, with increases in coverage area and average transmitted data rate of up to 50% in congested areas, which can be attributed to the relays' ability to provide additional coverage options to users currently served by RSUs. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other models is quantified by measuring the distance between decision boundaries, known as Euclidean distance to decision boundary (EDDB). In our experiments with various convolutional networks and datasets, EDDB surpasses other candidate metrics in effectively guiding the distillation process. Additionally, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation outperforms previous techniques when the original data is accessible and performs competitively when it isn't. The proposed method provides a reliable solution to a critical issue in deep learning. The study's code can be found at https://github.com/jbinc/decbbkd. EDDB can be accessed via the KnowledgeDistilllary at https://knowledge-distilllary.github.io/. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency. TuRaN has the added benefit of functioning without the need for external oscillators, thus enhancing its already high robustness against environmental factors. As a result, TuRaN is well-suited for a wide range of applications, including cryptography, modeling, and simulation, operating within a wide range of voltage intervals (10% to 20% lower than nominal) and exhibiting self-healing capabilities due to its ability to continue generating random numbers consistently. Furthermore, we show that TuRaN is capable of withstanding temporary overvoltage events lasting up to several microseconds at 400 nm and nanosecond-scale overvoltage events lasting up to 10 microseconds at 180 nm. In comparison to previous SRAM-based TRNGs, TuRaN outperforms existing solutions in terms of throughput, energy consumption, and latency. Consequently, TuRaN is an ideal solution for applications requiring a high throughput of random numbers at a relatively low energy cost with the capacity for continuous operation over long periods of time. The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a complete cancellation of spurious terms, and thus reducing the complexity in numerical evaluations. In this context, we introduce a modern framework for loop-tree duality, characterized by precise analytical manipulation of integral coefficients through single-particle correlations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying physics. Furthermore, we develop a numerical strategy, leveraging the principles of Monte Carlo sampling and optimization, to evaluate multi-loop integrals directly in momentum space, thereby enhancing numerical stability. The proposed framework is thoroughly tested against numerical results from established methods, including one-loop amplitude tools, for a range of planar and non-planar Feynman integrals across various kinematic regimes. The framework's performance is remarkable, exhibiting substantial numerical benefits, specifically up to two orders of magnitude improvement, in comparison to conventional methods. The framework's potential applications and extensions are also discussed to expand its scope and versatility. The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that significantly influence the Earth's cloud properties and radiative balance. In a cloud phenomenon called homogeneous nucleation, particles can form directly from oversaturated gas mixtures. Through extensive theoretical studies, the threshold concentrations for particle formation in binary mixtures of water and sulphuric acid have been extensively investigated. However, the studies often make unrealistic assumptions by treating vibrational motions as irrelevant. In reality, the zero-point motion can have a notable effect on the potential energy barriers and, consequently, the stability of the particle formation process. Therefore, we investigated the role of this motion in the nucleation of sulphuric acid-water vapour systems, focusing on three different energy levels for the associative formation of dimers. Our findings reveal that incorporating the zero-point motion for all atoms, as described by a semi-classical model, significantly alters the metastability thresholds and the energy barriers for the formation process, thereby making it more realistic. In the case of water-sulphuric acid dimer formation, the incorporation of the zero-point motion for all atoms led to a dramatic increase of about two orders of magnitude in the concentration threshold, bringing it into agreement with experimental findings. Consequently, we advocate for the incorporation of the zero-point motion in future theoretical studies on particle formation. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of accurately describing the kinetic energy in binary mixture systems, as the semi-classical treatment has a more limited impact. Finally, our research demonstrates that the application of quantum classical coherence, where the nucleus but not the electrons are treated quantum mechanically, has only a minor effect on the particle formation process. In contrast, the complete treatment of the kinetic energy as described by the semi-classical model has a much more profound impact. Interestingly, our research also sheds light on the structural properties of the sulphuric acid dimers, showing that the incorporation of the zero-point motion has a more pronounced effect on the distribution of sulfuric acid and water atoms than the quantum treatment of the valence electrons. In this regard, we found that the formation of close pairs, especially those with water and sulphuric acid, plays a crucial role and that the incorporation of the zero-point motion favours more compact, higher-energy configurations that are less susceptible to nucleation. Consequently, our research has a positive effect on the nucleation process, as the semi-classical model brings the concentration thresholds into agreement with experimental findings, whereas the quantum model has the opposite effect. In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity. Our findings are supported by experimental results showcasing the relationship between model parameters, its geometric complexity, and generalization performance. These outcomes have significant implications for training deep learning models, and our code is publicly available for reproduction of the experimental results. Our research also identifies key directions for further investigation. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.  Through our investigations, we analyzed various data augmentation techniques and assessed their impact on accuracy across different topics and the BERT-based model architecture.  The findings of our research revealed substantial improvements in accuracy following the application of data augmentation techniques, with gains as high as 93%.  Although the benefits of data augmentation were observed across all evaluated topics, the largest improvements were noted in topics encompassing more restrictive and specialized knowledge, suggesting data augmentation can be a potent tool in enhancing the performance of automated essay grading models, particularly when dealing with narrow domains.  In addition to illustrating the effectiveness of data augmentation across our base model of BERT, we also conducted comprehensive evaluations to determine the best data augmentation approach.  Our results indicate the superiority of the BERT-based model combined with BERT-Bigram and BERT-Isolated Word Lemma (BWL) over other data augmentation methods, including WL, WLK, and WLKS.  Consequently, we advocate for the use of BWL as a data augmentation approach when employing BERT-based models for automated essay grading.  Our research contributes to the ongoing efforts to develop sophisticated automated essay grading models.  The code used in this study is publicly accessible via the link: https://github.com/aman-007/Automated_Essay_Grading.  ESLQA, a BERT-based model augmented with BWL, has been deployed on the IBM Watson Platform and is accessible at the link provided above.  Our research demonstrates that data augmentation can significantly enhance the accuracy of automated essay grading models.  Consequently, we believe that data augmentation will play a crucial role in the ongoing development of sophisticated automated essay grading models.  Our findings also underscore the importance of comprehensive topic analysis to optimize the performance of data augmentation-based automated essay grading models.  Furthermore, our research illustrates the superiority of BWL over other data augmentation approaches

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context. Following the derivation of the wavefunction's exchange state through a sequence of unitary operations, the final transformation is found to depend on the parity of the total angular momentum. Consequently, for bosons, the wavefunction remains unchanged, whereas for fermions, the wavefunction becomes negated. Notably, this reasoning leads to fermions with half-integer spin exhibiting oscillating integer multiples of spin, along with a fundamental principle that dictates a particle's spin must be an half-integer multiple of $\hbar$. This reasoning also reveals its inherent connection to Pauli's theorem, which states that particles with integer spin are necessarily bosons. Finally, incorporating relativistic considerations via a Lorentz-invariant parity operator leads to the establishment of a connection between wavefunction parity and particle exchange statistics, as seen in the relativistic spin-statistics theorem. In conclusion, the notion of parity serves as the foundational principle underlying the spin-statistics connection in both non-relativistic and relativistic quantum theory. Furthermore, this study sheds new light on the inherent implications of the parity operation in quantum mechanics, which have hitherto not been recognized in the existing literature. Ultimately, this investigation demonstrates that the sign associated with particle permutation is a consequence of the wavefunction's exchange, rather than its sole determinant. In a particular application, the derivation of the wavefunction's exchange behavior is illustrated for bosonic and fermionic particles of arbitrary spin, along with fermions with half-integer spin. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that incorporates the benefits of RingCT and CNF-based accumulator techniques. The resulting Delegated RingCT protocol facilitates swift and cost-effective transactions, specifically with each transaction costing $O(\log n)$ operations and a cumulative price tag of $O(\log n)$ bytes. Furthermore, Delegated RingCT maintains the security attributes of RingCT, including unforgeable accumulators and hidden transaction values. To evidence transaction values, we utilize a single group element within an accumulator, followed by an accumulation of ring signatures via $\boldsymbol{\ell}$-delegated ring signatures. We maintain anonymity via hiding of ring signature components, achieved through a knapsack function and Schnorr proof. Delegated RingCT's computational efficiency is showcased via an integrated software framework, complemented by a practical example illustrating the scheme's ability to support numerous delegations. The specified parameters for Delegated RingCT, including accumulator and knapsack function module choices, as well as additional design requirements such as key management and update processes, are presented in the supplementary document. We believe Delegated RingCT to be an optimal solution for supporting efficient anonymous transactions within blockchain networks. The source code for Delegated RingCT can be accessed at https://github.com/ringct/delegated-ringct. The post is also available at https://bitcointechtalk.net/topic/168934/delegated-ringct. The public key used in the example can be found at https://bitcointalk.org/post-76411142.html#91511142. The private key used in the example can be accessed via https://pastebin.com/WE4eUkLi. The example transaction can be viewed at https://blockchain.visual.studio/com/delegated-ringct. Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of around 3.3 to 3.4 standard deviations and the measured rates of boson creation are also recorded.  The searches also put constraints on new physics beyond the standard model in which boson trilinear couplings could exist.  The measured rates of boson trilinear couplings have a strength that is up to 13.0 (expected to be 13.3) GeV/c^2, matching the predicted rates from the standard model to a precision of around 50%.  The constraints on exotic physics include the assumption that boson production occurs at a rate influenced by masses of approximately 5.3 (expected to be 5.5) TeV for a heavy vector boson with 90% W boson coupling similarity.  The detection and measurement of boson creation also allows the evaluation of predicted rates of boson decay patterns for massive particles that have not been detected yet.  Lastly, these measurements and the constraints on beyond-standard-physics have been updated with the data set's entire information. Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a wide range of network architectures and to predict multiple phenomena. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community to address increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method can enable sequential learning of multiple constitutive laws without memory loss and often with reduced data requirements, matching or exceeding the accuracy achieved through standard training of separate models for each law. Two popular continual learning techniques were tested and validated the effectiveness of the approach. The community now has the means to develop and share sophisticated mechanical models, leveraging neural networks' capabilities while overcoming longstanding limitations, thus marking a significant advancement in data-driven modeling. Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this framework by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also demonstrate that degree-degree correlations can be efficiently exploited to develop novel LDPC construction methods yielding superior performance compared to traditional degree distributions. Furthermore, our work is adaptable to various channel models and can be applied to evaluating the performance of LDPC-based systems in specific scenarios, such as interference-limited scenarios. We believe that this study will facilitate the development of novel LDPC construction methods that account for degree-degree correlations, yielding superior performance and improved system efficiency.

An advanced algorithm, known as the predictive safety filter, has been designed to enhance the software in automated vehicles by incorporating a safety layer. This algorithm works by generating a nominal trajectory for the vehicle to follow while taking into account any limitations and safety constraints. In the event of discrepancies between the nominal trajectory and the actual vehicle path, the safety algorithm activates corrective actions to ensure the vehicle stays on course. This study presents a novel predictive safety algorithm based on system level synthesis that incorporates continuous, time-varying safety constraints, such as those related to distance and speed. The algorithm is then evaluated using a simplified vehicle model under various conditions, including sudden changes in slope and friction surface. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm in preventing the vehicle from deviating from a safe path. Furthermore, the algorithm's computational efficiency was confirmed, as it only adds a fraction of a second to the existing navigation algorithm. This predictive safety filter offers a versatile solution that can be adapted for use in a range of safety-critical systems. A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as 80-channel interferometers, to compromise the advanced decoy-state QKD system. Specifically, the target system was the entanglement-based QKD system developed by Xie et al., which did not utilize full phase randomization in their source. Our findings indicate that the existing protection mechanisms against main channel attacks are insufficient to safeguard against our proposed attack. We have also demonstrated that the intensity distribution of our source can be formulated as a mixed model, and successfully recovered the entire source intensity setting. Consequently, the entanglement-based QKD system with partial phase randomization is susceptible to our attack, rendering it ineffective. Our research highlights the importance of utilizing full phase randomization in the source for secure quantum key distribution. Additionally, our work showcases the practical implementation of the source model in real-world QKD systems, and serves as a valuable reference for hacking experiments targeting QKD systems employing source intensity settings and phase randomization. Lastly, our study serves as a valuable guide for selecting suitable QKD systems and designing new quantum key distribution systems capable of withstanding quantum hacking attacks.
