The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying them to consider the passage of time. Our approach is straightforward: we create two sets of node embeddings, and these embeddings are updated based on the relative temporal positions of the nodes in the graph. Our method can be used with any static model of choice. Our evaluation compared the performance of SpliMe to that of a number of leading models, and the results indicate that this approach outperforms other models, and in some cases, significantly so. Furthermore, we found that utilizing the Widrow-Hoff learning rule can accelerate convergence, and that temporal regularization can improve the stability of the model. Finally, we created a new dataset, TKG-BBB, based on real-world data, and found that it presents a challenging case study for evaluating our approach. The proposed SpliMe method, as well as the associated dataset and code, are available for research purposes. Additionally, we created a web-based interface for generating visualizations related to our study. These resources can be accessed at https://tinyurl.com/54c8df5j. Our work offers several contributions: the development of a flexible, efficient, and effective method for encoding the passage of time in knowledge graphs; a new dataset based on real-world data, and characterized by a cooccurrence pattern that complicates link prediction tasks; and an analysis of the impact of temporal contexts on model performance. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions. Our findings indicate that the heavy quark potential's complex structure has a significant impact on its dissociation probability, particularly a wide dissociation area for certain quark energies in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Moreover, we observed that the anisotropic nature of the heavy quark potential causes dissociation probabilities to differ between along and perpendicular directions to the magnetic field. Our research will contribute to a deeper understanding of a system comprised of hot matter and a strong magnetic field, as found in certain types of stars and hypothetical objects known as quark stars. Our findings may also be useful in guiding experiments at future heavy-ion colliders, particularly those conducting experiments with nuclear magnets. Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce visually relevant high-fidelity sounds and generate these in under the time it takes for audio playback on a high-end graphics processing unit. We train a transformer that draws upon a codebook obtained from a variant of VQGAN optimized to produce compact spectral samples and utilizes a novel spectrogram-based quality measure. These spectral samples are transformed into waveforms using a window-based generator, which significantly enhances the generation speed. Since there are limited tools for automatically assessing the quality of synthesized soundscapes, we introduce FID and MKL, a new sensitivity metric derived from the multi-kernel learning technique that proves significantly more effective than traditional metrics like FID. Our model, with a sub-$3000$ graphics processing unit, outperforms previous approaches, including those with additional fine-tuning, in both quality and timescale. Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our IPO studio software. A practical case study on gesture recognition using IPO Deep Learning modules is also presented. Finally, best practice guidelines for implementing recurrent neural networks in practical applications are suggested. Finally, we present an overview of recurrent neural networks, suggest practical use cases, and offer best practice guidelines for implementation.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. Currently, analyzing and diagnosing issues within large datasets is challenging, especially when training models in an automated setting. To address this, we have created DataGANS, a tool that uses end-to-end machine learning pipelines to process datasets and identify problematic entries. Each entry's impact is calculated according to the Shapley value framework, taking into account the expected improvement when included, the total benefit when included, and the contribution to model loss. This allows data analysts to effectively prioritize and investigate individual data points. Our solution's efficacy is demonstrated in practical scenarios, such as identifying and correcting label errors, extracting sensitive information, and detecting manipulations in review ratings, and it outperforms the competing methods in accuracy, efficiency, and user interaction metrics. This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices. Our findings can be illustrated through examples from combinatorics, statistics, and topology, which will provide an alternative perspective on already well-known results. Furthermore, this study sets the stage for future investigations into generalized polynomial families derived from semi-infinite algebraic K-theory. One of our key contributions is the enumeration of a specific class of combinatorial objects, known as Laminations, in a linear matrix space context. This involves generating functions that relate to the partial flag variety of a semisimple Lie group, specifically in a regime where sizes of both the flag and partial flag varieties become infinitely large. Our analysis draws from the framework of transverse geometry, an area that studies discrete invariants from this point of view. Our work on Laminations is a fundamental exploration that is expected to yield significant developments in related fields. one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as the
prevalent approach for RE. In particular, the reliability of DNNs in the forms of
supervised and distant supervision methods makes them highly sought-after solutions
for RE. This article serves as an introduction, offering an in-depth analysis of DNNs in
RE from two primary angles: supervised RE and distant supervision RE. It also covers
the emergence of new approaches, recent trends, and prospective avenues for further
research in the area of RE. Our intention is for this article to serve as a comprehensive
reference for researchers engaged in NLP, particularly those working with DNNs in RE.

RE, presented at Conferences NE-2020 and ICSRA-2019. Due to space constraints, some
parts of the article have been initially presented in those works. This article presents
a revised version, featuring comprehensive updates.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and provide valuable insights into the inherent limitations of hypergraph reconstruction. Our method also surpasses state-of-the-art graph embedding-based baselines in multiple evaluations, showcasing its superiority in analyzing complex system data. This research will be facilitated through an open-source toolkit, HRe. Its source code and additional information can be accessed at https://github.com/cuiyanlin4/SupHVRE.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. Lastly, we successfully applied this concept to analyze experimental polar far-field images of two commonly used microcavity lasers. Our approach not only offers a more precise method for evaluating directional emission but also a systematic way to analyze complex structures. This technique can also be utilized as a resource for refining design and optimization strategies of microcavity lasers that operate under wedge or cone emission configurations. It's also scalable to one-dimensional photonic structures and can be applied to evaluate emission directionality in a wider range of photonic products and devices. Overall, this research presents an innovative, versatile, and advanced method for evaluating emission directionality that could significantly contribute to the development and design of future photonic products and their applications.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the main challenge lies in accurately extracting the defect area from the fabric's texture features. To address this, an algorithm combining low-rank decomposition and sparse representation is devised to segregate the background and defect components. First, the texture image is transformed into directional gradient representation through GHOG, which represents each fabric pattern as a directional gradient component. Subsequently, the codebook is generated from this representation. Next, the algorithm seeks the low-rank matrix and sparse components in the generated codebook. Ultimately, the background and defect components are extracted through sparse reconstruction. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this approach successfully differentiates background and defect areas even with varying pattern orientations. Additionally, due to its robust low-rank matrix decomposition, this method remains resilient to natural variations in fabric patterns, making it effective in a wide range of fabric types. A comparison with state-of-the-art methods, including SRR, LRD, and SpR, reveals a significant performance boost of 3.66% to 41.11% in terms of accuracy. Therefore, this proposed method exhibits superior detachment of background and defect components, as well as precise defect area segmentation. The study includes an evaluation of different GHOG parameter settings and 16 different fabric types to ensure its reliability and versatility. The method has been made available through an open-source MATLAB toolbox at the provided URL. This approach's ability to accurately detect defects has numerous practical implications, including fabric inspection, where the method can be applied to various types of fabrics with minimal modifications. Furthermore, this study's direction-sensitive descriptor technique has potential applications in other image processing tasks that involve directional data, such as road sign classification and facial landmark detection. In summary, this defect detection algorithm, comprising GHOG and low-rank decomposition with sparse representation, presents a comprehensive solution to the defect segmentation challenge, exhibiting superior performance and practical applications. The study contributes to the literature by leveraging GHOG and low-rank decomposition to achieve high-precision defect detection and segmentation. The open-source MATLAB toolbox has been made available at the provided URL for both educational and practical use. This includes the complete source code and data sets. The study evaluates GHOG with different parameter settings and 16 different fabric types to ensure its reliability and versatility.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS. These case studies reveal that while real-time data is ideal, infrequent data updates can still facilitate the detection of incidents within a reasonable time frame. Crucially, this method avoids the analysis of system states, thereby ensuring safe operation and preventing potential protection malfunctions. Our tests confirm that this method can accurately detect incidents in specified scenarios. Specifically, it can identify up to 90% of active power control incidents and 85% of reactive power control incidents. Furthermore, it can predict incident occurrence with a reliability of 87.5% for both active and reactive power control. Our research is groundbreaking because it introduces a data-driven method for identifying critical incidents in smart distribution networks, thereby enhancing the reliability of the power grid. Additionally, this method is characterized by its simplicity, thereby facilitating its implementation across a wide range of distribution networks. While this work focuses on identifying incidents in ESS, the proposed method can be easily adapted to detect incidents in other advanced systems used in modern distribution networks. Ultimately, this work is centered on improving the reliability of the power grid through data-driven incident detection. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.

On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our results demonstrate the efficacy of five practical techniques for accelerating text-based game simulations.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this information from human to robot systems has been overlooked. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap with a new method to transfer manipulability information from one robot to another with a different kinematic structure. Since these ellipsoids are based on symmetric positive-definite matrices, they can be treated as points on a specific geometric manifold. This work offers the first approach to transfer manipulability by leveraging the technique of point cloud registration. To achieve this, it employs an algorithm combining parallel transport with Iterative Closest Point. The method also uses an adaptive geometric matching heuristic to find corresponding features in manipulability ellipsoids. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated through simulation studies involving simple manipulators as well as 7-DoF models replicating human arm anatomy. The results show significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art approaches. With increased training data, it demonstrates consistent and robust transfer of manipulability ellipsoids, ultimately facilitating faster teaching of complex robots. The proposed method has been made available through an open-source software platform. Additionally, detailed virtual demos have been made accessible through a user-friendly interface. The software and demos can be accessed via the following links: \url{https://robot-learning.org/experiments/manipulability_transfer/}, \url{https://robot-learning.org/experiments/manipulability_transfer/?tab=code}. A video summarizing the paper's content has also been included: \url{https://robot-learning.org/publications/mulcahy2022manipulability/}. The transfer of manipulability ellipsoids has numerous potential applications, particularly in areas such as robotics, neuroscience, and computer vision. The (as of yet unsolved) problem of efficiently transferring this information from humans to robots will likely have far-reaching implications for the development of more advanced robot systems. This research aims to provide an important contribution towards resolving this issue. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection and feature matching methods yields surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimations in such video footage. The proposed method, which consists of two stages, initially learns a canonical pose from multiple videos, followed by a model for predicting object poses in a single view. In contrast to existing top-tier models, this method performs competitively without relying on explicit 3D pose annotations during the training process. Additionally, we present the Accidental Turntables Dataset, a set of challenging images depicting 41,212 car scenarios with complex backgrounds, motion blur, and varying lighting conditions, serving as a new benchmark for 3D pose estimation. The code, dataset, and model weights can be accessed via https://github.com/yangweikai/Accidental Turntables. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing single-view 3D pose estimation models on both our new dataset and two other standard benchmarks, achieving the most robust performance improvement when 3D pose annotations are scarce. While this method is specifically designed for objects rotated in a circle (e.g. cars), we have found that it also performs reasonably well on objects not rotated in a circle (e.g. planes), albeit with reduced accuracy. Therefore, this could be an interesting approach for training 3D pose estimation models even in scenarios where the rotation is not explicit. The method will be made available as a plugin for the DeepObjectLasso software, allowing users to leverage existing modern single-view 3D pose estimation models within this framework. The plugin will be made available upon the acceptance of this manuscript. On a dataset of car images, we have found that our method can predict the 3D pose with an average error of 3.99cm, comparable to the state-of-the-art models that were trained using expensive LiDAR data (4.17cm), as well as other models that were trained using other forms of weak supervision (6.25cm), revealing its robustness in predicting object poses when other forms of data are unavailable. Similarly, on two standard benchmarks for single-view 3D pose estimation, we have found that our method can predict the 3D pose with an average error of 7.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, outperforming other current approaches. Experiments were conducted on the recently created CoVaxLies dataset, a comprehensive collection of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation gathered from Twitter discussions. This new dataset allows us to distinguish which specific types of misinformation are more commonly accepted and which are more commonly disputed. Our innovative neural framework demonstrates the significant impact social media theories have on the dissemination of misinformation. This work sets the stage for future research aimed at addressing the root cause of misinformation dissemination, thus potentially mitigating its harmful effects. Ultimately, this research aims to develop intelligent systems capable of discerning the specific types of misinformation that are more widely adopted and those that are more widely disputed. In doing so, we hope to utilize these intelligent systems to gauge public sentiment regarding various misinformation types and thereby leverage that insight to combat misinformation dissemination. This approach could ultimately enable the development of intelligent systems capable of addressing the spread of misinformation. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish that solutions with positive energy will persist indefinitely. A key element in our proof is the extension of a previously established approach from the literature, adapted to account for the presence of the obstacle. The obstacle problem presents a complex mathematical challenge, rendering the proof rather intricate and difficult to navigate. For this reason, we have chosen to present the proof in the appendix, in order to streamline the main body of the discussion and focus on the key physical and mathematical implications of our solution, as well as the intricate relationship between the solutions and the geometric shape of the obstacle. The latter aspect, in particular, is crucial to understanding the global behavior of the solutions and holds significant analytical value. As predicted by the celebrated Skyrme model in condensed matter physics, the interaction between the solutions and the obstacle can give rise to remarkably diverse and intricate patterns of behavior. The solutions can take on a diverse array of shapes, influenced as they are by the intricate geometry of the obstacle and the complex interplay of energy interactions. In this paper, we embark on a comprehensive analysis of this diverse array of solutions and their behavior under the influence of the nonlinear interaction and the geometric shape of the obstacle. The solutions can be categorized into various groups based on different symmetry conditions and the energy properties of the solutions, and we examine each of these groups in detail, exploring the solutions, their behavior over time, and the geometric shape of the solutions. The solutions will either persist indefinitely, or the solutions will collapse within a finite time period, and we examine all possible scenarios. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution mechanism and a memory layer to facilitate sampling point generation. This method is inspired by the goal of producing training points that accurately reflect the solution field while also incorporating the inherent structure in the solution. We evaluate RANG in comparison to traditional sampling methods, and find that it successfully produces a diverse set of training points which result in improved training efficiency and accurate predictions for both linear and nonlinear scenarios. The implementation of RANG is accompanied by comprehensive source code. Further details are available online.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, and that a computationally efficient self-consistent equation can accurately describe this phenomenon. To validate our approach, we compare our simulation results with existing experimental data, and find a strong correlation between the simulated domain map and the observed negative capacitance in the current-voltage characteristics. Furthermore, we explore how the domain wall induced negative capacitance affects the scaling delay in a 2nm technology node, and find that the effect significantly contributes to it. Our study lays the foundation for developing a complete 3D multi-domain device simulator that can accurately model these dynamic processes, and enables the further optimization of nanoferroelectric devices. Additionally, we propose a novel task to determine the material properties of ferroelectric films, where the ferroelectric film and the surrounding metal gate are modeled as coupled systems. We find that the interaction between the two is the dominant factor in determining the system's response, and that the constraints on the coupled system enable us to derive two key equations that can retrieve the essential properties of the ferroelectric material through iterative minimization. As a proof-of-concept, we use this approach to calculate the switching energy of a FeFET with a 2nm transition width. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of multi-domain ferroelectric materials and their application in nanoferroelectric devices. The simulated results show that the negative capacitance effect, which is induced by the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material, significantly contributes to the performance of these devices. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational cost, with a significant reduction in model complexity. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical issues related to low-energy fusion measurements are addressed. These concerns revolve around the utility of multiplicity filtering as a standard tool in analyzing fusion cross sections obtained through the Trojan horse method. This method involves separating protons of varying energies and multiplicities. However, using this approach may lead to an underestimation of measured fusion yields. Another area of concern is the employment of the phenomenological barrier parameterization. This approach is used to extract both the Coulomb and non Coulomb barriers from measured proton energies. Although the non Coulomb barrier associated with the carbon-carbon system is relatively small, its correct value is crucial for an accurate understanding of the astrophysical $S$ factor. Another critical aspect is the electronic excitation of the product nucleus during the fusion process. Although the contribution of such excitation is generally minor, it becomes more significant at lower energy ranges. A more realistic estimation of these contributions is achieved through the employment of the coupled reaction method. This approach has been successfully used to analyze experimental data from the range of 15 to 25 MeV relative energy and has provided a thorough understanding of the role of multiplicity filtering, phenomological barrier parameterization, and electronic excitation in this energy range. Furthermore, this approach has allowed for an accurate calculation of the $S$ factor for the carbon-carbon system up to an energy of 20 MeV, and has enabled a direct comparison of the calculated $S$ factor with the measured values. Based on this comparison, it is concluded that the measured $S$ factor values are underestimated due to the experimental limitations associated with multiplicity filtering and phenomological barrier parameterization. Therefore, these experimental limitations should be removed in future measurements, and the $S$ factor values should be analyzed through the employment of the coupled reaction method over an energy range that is more representative of the conditions found in astrophysical environments. Finally, several suggestions and guidelines for future research are provided to facilitate the further development of the Trojan horse method. Specifically, it is proposed that future research should focus on the determination of the $S$ factor at energies below 20 MeV, and should also involve a new analytical approach based on the coupled reaction method and the microscopic Coulomb barrier. This approach has been successfully used in the analysis of low energy fusion measurements and has allowed for an accurate understanding of the role of tunneling in the fusion process. A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, our exploration of this devolatilisation model's boundaries and variation in planetary mass and size highlights the potential diversity of internal structures in terrestrial exoplanets. By combining precise star abundances, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, our study advances understanding of terrestrial exoplanets, particularly those similar to Earth, and may influence future mission priorities in searching for life-supporting worlds. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred solution for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can help, but it is challenging to obtain optimal performance. Our work focuses on enhancing the robustness and accuracy of CSI-based localization by leveraging attention mechanisms within the DNN. By concentrating computation on the most relevant CSI channels for location prediction, the network's generalization to diverse environments is improved. Experiments on both an indoor campus dataset and a publicly available outdoor dataset show that our solution outperforms conventional DNNs by a margin of 0.10 to 0.20 in location accuracy. Detailed evaluation and analysis of the attention-based DNN are also provided to facilitate further research. Since our method incorporates channel selection, it is applicable to various CSI-based localization schemes. Therefore, the presented approach can be easily integrated into existing localization systems to enhance their performance. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. By employing this categorical approach, we can efficiently analyze both the intrinsic structure of the modal language itself and the category theoretical framework, as well as the relationship between different expansions of the modal language through the topological structures in their respective categories. In particular, we will focus on the symmetric, monoidal, closed structure in our topological categories, which allows us to make explicit the relationships between different types of modal logics through the category theoretical framework. In future papers, we plan to demonstrate how this categorical structure can be used to guide cut-free proof calculi construction for various expansions of modal logic by translating cut elimination into the category theoretical framework. Moreover, we will outline a method for extending our approach to more complex linguistic frameworks with infinite compositions and degenerate modalities, and provide an illustrative example of this extension for the basic S5 logic. Finally, we will outline the scope of our methodology for mapping modal logic semantics to topological categories, and predict that it will be an effective tool in analyzing a wide range of modal logics. Although our methodology is generally applicable to both first-order and higher-order modal logic expansions, our initial application will focus on basic S5 logic for simplicity's sake. Throughout the paper, we use the names of topological categories to denote both the categories themselves and their underlying structures. Additionally, we assume a working knowledge of modal logic and the topological categories theory, as well as familiarity with categorical logic. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2013 this was contested. We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 2, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and establish a characterization for those with such a minimum. In addition, we provide a lower bound on the size of the support for any function satisfying a given spectral constraint, and we investigate its closeness to being tight. Our results generalize previous work on functions defined on the vertices of the hypercube Q^n, and our generalization to the Hamming graphs H(n,q) also incorporates a recent study of Meckes and Tilson. The present work draws on materials from the 2020 fall semester courses 18T12: Algebraic methods in combinatorics and 18.419 Sala de Recinto Online Principles of Combinatorics. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing access to a model database with pre-configured settings for optimal exploration. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/. In conjunction with this release, we also distributed COPASI 4.24, incorporating several major improvements, including enhanced binary compatibility, improved grid management, and updated visualization options. Furthermore, ShinyCOPASI and COPASI 4.24 include an innovative task for frequency distribution analysis, allowing users to run this task in parallel using available CPU cores. To facilitate updates and a centralized model library, we established a website at https://models.copasi.org/ offering a collection of models that can be easily accessed through ShinyCOPASI. Models can also be contributed to this library by submitting them to https://tasks.copasi.org/. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework. In a notable finding, no single method surpasses all others in addressing uncertainty quantification, highlighting both the necessity for continued research in this area and the immediate utility of the presented framework for solving numerous applications. Ultimately, this work seeks to establish a common language and standard for evaluating and enhancing NN-based solutions to physics and engineering problems involving uncertainty quantification. The presented framework is expected to contribute significantly to resolving issues in these fields and will serve as a standard for comparing and combining various deep neural network techniques. The framework's code and research results are openly available on GitHub at: https://github.com/ugd-uqff/UQFramework. The repository will be regularly updated with new methods, hyperparameters, and data to foster collaboration and facilitate the use of this framework for ongoing research in uncertainty quantification using NNs. Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP. Moreover, its memory usage is 0.9 GB, significantly lower than the alternative partial policy iteration with 16 states, which used 13 GB. Consequently, inexact GMRES policy iteration successfully combines the efficacy of partial policy iteration and the efficiency of inexact policy iteration, thereby representing the best algorithm for our knowledge in reducing the computational cost of policy iteration while maintaining a comparable rate of convergence. Moreover, inexact GMRES policy iteration is versatile, having been tested in both continuous and discrete settings, thereby exhibiting a high degree of applicability. In continuation, a refined inexact policy iteration algorithm will be designed to exhibit an improved rate of convergence. For instance, inexact policy iteration based on the incomplete Cholesky decomposition will be shown to converge at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of iterations, thereby surpassing inexact GMRES policy iteration in this regard. Nonetheless, it will be outperformed by inexact policy iteration based on the incomplete LU decomposition with a preconditioner, which will be shown to converge at a rate proportional to the number of iterations, thereby exhibiting the fastest known rate of convergence among all algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees. Therefore, inexact policy iteration based on the incomplete LU decomposition with a preconditioned GMRES will be shown to converge at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of iterations, while maintaining a linear computational cost, thereby exhibiting a critical combination of efficiency and efficacy. This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios. The results show that this approach significantly reduces the computational cost without sacrificing precision when applied to time series data, and its performance is largely determined by the frequency of selected key points. The study includes an in-depth analysis of the produced parameter distributions and suggests that future work should focus on using these distributions to improve the representation of parameter uncertainty in model output. The proposed technique is made available under an open-source license, and the code for replicating the study's results can be found at https://github.com/julianatz/mce4ts. This research is an extension of initial findings reported in a shorter publication (Tzouanas et al., 2022). Key improvements include the development of a more efficient approximation of multi-dimensional parameter distributions using contaminated normal distributions, and a comprehensive comparison with other methods on a range of problems, including exponential and multi-variate exponential models. Additionally, the study includes an analysis of the frequency of key points and suggests that future work should focus on using these points to identify and model abrupt changes in time series, such as shifts or changes in parameter behavior. The study's methodology is versatile and can be applied to a range of problems, including climate modeling and evaluating the reliability of experimental measurements. Future work should focus on using the proposed technique to improve the efficiency of climate model evaluations, and on developing new algorithms to identify and model changes in time series data. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries (LMQs), where the learner can verify the labels of nearby points to the training sample. We found, however, that LMQs alone are not enough to increase the robustness threshold for conjunctions and its various superclasses, such as decision lists and halfspaces. To address this issue, we developed a new local equivalence query (LEQ) oracle, which allows the learner to confirm whether a model's hypothesis and the target concept agree within a certain range, in addition to providing any existing counterexamples. We established a crucial separation result: while we found that robust learning is generally impossible for many concept classes if the learner's query radius is significantly smaller than the adversary's allowed perturbation budget, our research also identified the conditions under which we can successfully develop robust ERM algorithms. We subsequently calculated the number of local queries required to execute these algorithms using the principles of online learning. Additionally, we further optimized the number of required queries for conjunctions. Our paper culminates with the creation of robust learning algorithms for halfspaces under different settings. The main challenge in developing these algorithms is the number of local queries needed to ensure that the learner's model and the target concept agree on all training samples, a problem that arises due to the infinite possible perturbations affecting the model's input. To address this issue, we developed a new non-constructive approach, proving the existence of a model that can be learned robustly, while also establishing a bound on the number of local queries required. The outcome is a robust ERM algorithm for halfspaces using at most $O\left((\frac{d}{\epsilon^2})\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$ local queries, a result that is closer to being optimal than previous approaches. Furthermore, we successfully modified this algorithm to work in the $L_\infty$ setting, achieving a robust accuracy of $2\epsilon$ instead of $3\epsilon$ while using the same number of queries. The experiment was performed twice using materials from different locations on Mars and the Moon, and the results were compared to real rock samples from those planets, showing that our method can produce samples with similar internal structures and strength to the actual rocks from Mars and the Moon. Notably, the strength of these materials peaked at a compression strength of 3.53 MPa and a tension strength of 0.19 MPa, and fire expansion of 3.55%. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. By accounting for uncertainties in observing these lines under diverse conditions, we estimate a $\sim$0.6 M$_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$ error in the predicted star formation rates, which is similar to the expected precision of these predictions without this observational constraint. Overall, our study suggests that the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$s line might be a valuable data point in predicting star formation rates that are accurate to within 0.6 M$_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$ in a range of galaxy types. The associated code and data can be found at https://github.com/sdprice/prospector_test_paper/tree/br67. Future work will investigate other indicators like this that could improve the precision of these predictions. The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field. In this paper, the newly found solution is explored in-depth, its approximations are accented, as well as its limitations, mainly being confined to a limited time frame. In comparison, the alternating diffusion process reveals the precise nature of solutions to the general diffusion equation, a property which the Fisher-KPP equation clearly lacks. Consequently, time maps and the invariance of singular manifolds for the Fisher-KPP equation need to be re-evaluated. In addition, the presented approach can be easily modified to tackle more complex equations, such as the combined reaction-diffusion equations for multiple species, as long as they adhere to a particular linear diffusion framework. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Furthermore, we identify that the incorporation of acoustic features into the model can improve duration prediction, particularly for shorter phones. With its potential to model long-duration sequences, this new method paves the way for enhanced speech synthesis quality. The proposed system has been made available on GitHub. Speech synthesized using this system has been submitted to the DACAH evaluation platform. Additionally, we have obtained an ISRC code for our dataset. More details on implementation, data preparation, and training procedures are available upon request to the corresponding author. 

Keywords: statistical speech synthesis, duration modelling, median-based approach, recursive neural networks, speech features.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the fundamental single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive functionalities for simulating data, testing models, verifying predictions, evaluating model performance, and making predictions on unseen data. Through a case study and a tutorial, this package demonstrates its capabilities by estimating species abundance in two distinct bird habitats: eastern USA's bird population and a forest ecosystem in New Hampshire, thereby providing a practical approach to address data inaccuracies and spatial relationships even for extensive datasets. To obtain an accurate Hubble constant from type Ia supernovae with high redshift, it's crucial to account for variations in light curves and spectra. Our approach introduces a probabilistic autoencoder model that effectively learns and predicts residual sine histories for supernovae, utilizing both cosine-based and smoothed sine-based models for the temporal evolution of omega-equation of state (ω) in supernovae spectra. By employing a structured model that incorporates multiple layers of hierarchical Gaussian processes, we can learn complex patterns in spectra and represent the relationship between supernovae properties in a reduced-dimensional space. Our results show that the representation learned by the autoencoder is sufficient to explain observations in the sample, and we perform a Bayesian analysis to estimate key parameters, including the dark energy equation of state at high redshift. Our research aims to facilitate further investigations into cosmological applications of the model, such as determining the Hubble constant. Our code is available on GitHub for public use. Our research is the first to apply a probabilistic autoencoder to a colletion of type Ia supernovae data, especially with regards to spectral time-series data that is particularly data-hungry. Our study demonstrates that a reduced-dimensional representation of the data can be learned from the type Ia supernovae dataset, without making any assumptions about the relations between the variables involved. Our research provides a valuable contribution to the development of precision cosmology by introducing a versatile statistical tool that can effectively capture and describe temporal spectral histories of supernovae with varying parameters. Our approach gives equal consideration to two popular models for sine histories, offering a comprehensive comparison and learning experience. Our research has significant implications for applying deep learning techniques to cosmology, even with limited observational data, and demonstrates that a high-dimensional representation of the data can be learned using our approach, with applications in other fields such as meteorology and medicine. Our study outperforms other machine learning models, and our hierarchical Gaussian process model provides a flexible and efficient framework for learning and extending the model. Our research has successfully eliminated the need for pre-supernovae model components in the sine-based model, and our structured model has shown that the representation learned is sufficient to explain observations in the sample. Our results provide accurate estimates for parameters such as the equation of state at high redshift. Our code is available on GitHub for public use. Our research has successfully applied a deep learning technique to cosmological data for the first time, and our hierarchical Gaussian process model has been successfully applied to type Ia supernovae data. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by differential rotation.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, depending on the angular velocity and anti-solar differential rotation angles. However, in anti-solar dynamos, global polarity reversals are restricted to specific limits. Furthermore, quasi-linear dynamos experience reduced magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, and are less dependent on parameters. Additionally, our studies in semi-global dynamos reveal that global polarity reversals are mostly confined to rotation alone, while local dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals across various rotation regimes.

These findings indicate that anti-solar differential rotation can lead to reduced magnetic activity and an increased likelihood of quenched magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals. Consequently, we can exclude some rapidly rotating stars as suitable candidates for hosting long-lasting magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals, and instead, expand the scope for these phenomena in slow rotators. Lastly, our studies provide a foundation for future research into the observational links between differential rotation and magnetic activity, as well as global polarity reversals, and provide invaluable insights into the design of future observational and numerical studies. They also offer a framework towards understanding the intricate, complex relationships between differential rotation and magnetic activity, and provide a potential explanation for the relatively low occurrence of long-lasting magnetic cycles and global polarity reverses in various rotating stars. We undertook a study to evaluate the effectiveness of these limitations in mitigating the spread of misinformation. Utilizing network architecture similar to that of WhatsApp, we developed a system for simulating user interactions and message propagation, as well as a comprehensive dataset containing a wide range of English topics. We selected topics related to COVID-19 and comparable topics not associated with the pandemic, such as weather forecasts, to conduct our research. Conversely, users find alternative strategies to overcome these limitations, such as splitting long messages into smaller parts. Ultimately, our research suggests that simply imposing technical restrictions on message forwarding is an insufficient solution to addressing the complex problem of misinformation dissemination. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in its performance. Furthermore, our analysis suggested that the success of our AI relied on its ability to store and retrieve information, particularly its ability to recall recent selections when given a binary input. By incorporating a specialized memory module, known as the Memory-based Revere Link, which could prioritize and retain select information, our AI was able to achieve high levels of accuracy without any guidance or hand-engineered solutions. The outstanding performance of our AI, coupled with the insights gained from its trackable progress, offered valuable insights into the underlying mechanics of counting. Consequently, our work provided a promising foundation for future research in areas such as AI-driven hypothesis testing and the formulation of new mathematical theories. By combining cutting-edge AI techniques with the scrutiny of cognitive science, we were able to recreate the core elements of counting, making our findings relevant to the ongoing quest to develop truly intelligent machines that think abstractly. Bloom filters provide quick approximations, but they can be inaccurate at high speeds. An alternative, Bloom filters' cousin, the Cuckoo filter, offers better efficiency but still unreliable at high throughput. Both filters suffer from a trade-off between speed, space, and precision. However, their trade-off can be harsh, especially for high-throughput systems. To address this, we introduce a new class of approximate membership filters, xorfilters, with a distinct property: the exact opposite of efficient algorithms results in more accurate approximations. Unlike Bloom and Cuckoo filters, which use efficient hash functions, xorfilters use less efficient hash functions, making them 30% faster and 40% more accurate or use significantly less space for the same accuracy level. From a theoretical standpoint, we prove that Bloom and Cuckoo filters cannot achieve both higher accuracy and faster processing speeds or use less storage while maintaining the same accuracy. Nevertheless, we present an exception, xorfilters, that breaks this limitation, offering versatility in design and a wide range of possible hash functions. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate the substantial performance gains of xorfilters over traditional filters, making them suitable for numerous high-speed applications, such as networking, storage, and simulation. Ultimately, xorfilters may become a more attractive option than Bloom and Cuckoo filters due to their superior efficiency. To facilitate the adoption of xorfilters, we open-source our implementation and make it available for online use. Additionally, we provide a mathematical justification for choosing the specific hash functions used in our experimental evaluation. Lastly, our results suggest an answer to an open problem from 2009, asking whether it is possible to create approximate membership filters with a false positive rate of $o(\ln p/\ln (1-p))$. We can accurately calculate this rate only if $p$ is known in advance; otherwise, a more conservative estimate applies. When possible, we can achieve an approximately $k$-wise false positive rate, and our filters remain not only efficient but also surprisingly resilient to hash function fluctuations, making our design more flexible than expected. Lastly, we open-source our implementation to facilitate adoption. To validate the uniqueness of hash values in Bloom and Cuckoo filters, we use random hash functions. However, in many applications, the availability of random hash functions is limited, and non-random hash functions must be used instead. We present a theoretical analysis of how our filter class performs when these less random hash functions are employed, demonstrating that our xorfilters remain efficient, accurate

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, we delve into the constraints imposed by the continuity principle in convex geometry, revealing them to be analogous to L\"ewy's fundamental problem in complex geometry. We conclude by analyzing the first main theorem of Nevanlinna theory and its divisorial extension, drawing parallels with the P\'olya-Herglotz inequality from convex geometry. This intersection of concepts from convex geometry and algebraic geometry offers fresh insights into the latter, as exemplified by the divisors with finite singularities. Our work likely holds significance beyond the scope of projective varieties, expanding to non-necessarily projective K\"ahler manifolds with a fixed bounded curvature. The paper concludes by outlining related directions for future research. One such area of inquiry is the extension of our results to the more general category of almost-positive line bundles. The potential for growth in this field is substantial, given the novel connections between convex geometry and complex geometry that have been established here. The research presented in this study is original and has not been published elsewhere. The main text is accessible to a broad audience of mathematicians with basic knowledge of algebraic and convex geometry, whereas the appended materials assume a higher level of expertise. The proofs provided in the main text and the appended materials can serve as a research outline for new investigators. The primary tools employed in this investigation are from convex geometry, as well as the foundational concepts of algebraic and complex geometry. The specific techniques utilized include those from mixed volume theory, first Chern class additivity, and the continuity principle. The key results that enable our examination of the relationships between these concepts are the Heron mean, the P\'olya-Herglotz inequality, the first main theorem of Nevanlinna theory, and the divisors with finite singularities. The conclusions derived can be extended to nearly positive line bundles. The manuscript includes a comprehensive bibliography

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values. This methodology has been successfully applied to technical analysis, yielding significant insights into market behavior and allowing for the quantification of volatility fluctuations over varying time spans. Notably, it has been observed that past market patterns tend to repeat in the future, although the extent of these repeats may be subject to prediction errors. This approach provides a quantitative assessment of the relative impact of past market activity on future trends. By considering both price stability and change, this method goes beyond traditional trend analysis, which typically relies on a single approach. The use of this trend analysis both with and without prediction errors allows for a comprehensive understanding of market dynamics. This new approach is based on advanced statistical models and is referred to as the Multiple Time Frame (MTF) method. A key aspect of this method involves quantifying the tendency of past markets to replicate in the future, an attribute known as market memory. This market memory is expressed as a fraction representing the ratio of useful past data to total historical data and is calculated using advanced signal processing techniques. The use of this approach has yielded substantial gains in trend analysis, exceeding those achieved with traditional technical analysis. As an independent approach, MTF analysis provides fresh perspectives on past and future market dynamics. Although based on established concepts such as dynamic price equations and market memory, this new method offers a comprehensive understanding of how present market behavior influences the future. A key trend analysis technique derived from this approach is called Market Momentum. This algorithm uses past and future price data to identify the state of highest trading efficiency and determine time frames that contribute to market momentum. By considering both price stability and change, this algorithm goes beyond traditional momentum analysis and provides a more comprehensive understanding of market dynamics. Another trend analysis technique derived from this approach is called Market Noise. This algorithm uses past and future price data to identify time frames with inconsistent trading activity and determine their impact on future trends. By combining the Market Momentum and Market Noise algorithms, researchers can study the dynamics of past and future markets, yielding new insights into market behavior. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server. In particular, it achieves a balance between robustness and performance similar to the current leading approach, while surpassing it in terms of maintaining user privacy. Notably, our framework achieves a significant improvement in running efficiency by a factor of up to 57.04 compared to the existing state-of-the-art. This is particularly notable as the evaluation was conducted on low-power IoT hardware. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Chen-ITSL/FLVoogd. A video explaining our approach can be found at https://youtu.be/IEs4H5YIv4k. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement of a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being essential for the latter process. These distinct conditions result in the formation of distinct features in the near-UV to red optical spectra of transiting exoplanets, especially those involving the absorption of starlight by metals in the atmosphere above the photosphere and the appearance of absorption features in the blue part of the spectrum due to residual H2 and He atmospheres. Therefore, we propose that small, temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets with masses less than 10 bars can be identified through transit observations that showcase distinctive signatures in their blue spectra, distinguishing them from those with massive H2/He envelopes, regardless of their size or irradiance level. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. The model's learning rule is compatible with the standard binary McCulloch-Pitts model, allowing it to efficiently retrieve stored patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals that the model exhibits robust pattern retrieval even with high levels of noise, and demonstrates robust binary sequence learning capabilities on various data sets. Importantly, our results indicate that the model can efficiently learn long binary sequences using short, localized synaptic weights, making it suitable for large-scale neural hardware implementation. Due to its binary nature, our model offers significant advantages over traditional real-valued neural network methods in terms of computational efficiency and the potential for biological plausibility.
