This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable predictions when encountering unseen text. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2D cycles in the Swift-Hohenberg equation. The proposed methodology can be applied to a broad range of systems described by partial and ordinary differential equations. Furthermore, this approach is independent of equation type and can be applied to dynamic systems defined by arbitrary maps. A significant adaptation of this methodology's concepts enables the analysis of probability distributions associated with solution sets in parameter-dependent solution tracking problems. This involves the precise calculation of probability density functions for solution tracking problems and their visualization, using the Lorenz equations as a practical example, where we calculate a probability density function for solutions of the Lorenz equations under discontinuous forcing. The proposed methodology, described in this study, opens up new avenues for the analysis of dynamic systems with parameters drawn randomly from specified intervals. The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. This work aims to develop an adaptive monitoring system capable of handling high-dimensional data in resource-scarce environments where various potential failures may occur. Our proposed solution incorporates the Shiryaev-Roberts method at the failure mode level and employs multi-arm bandit strategies to balance discovery and exploitation. Furthermore, our algorithm's theoretical underpinnings demonstrate its efficacy in isolating the primary failure mode. Through simulations and case studies, we verify that the detection performance of changes and accuracy in isolating the failure mode can be substantially enhanced. Ultimately, our approach offers substantial cost savings by minimizing unnecessary observations when no changes occur. The methodology's versatility allows it to be applied in a range of domains beyond industrial monitoring. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/naikmis/APOSDAI. We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to mimic galaxy growth patterns, is based on the concept of building these galaxies from numerous smaller celestial bodies formed in a uniform rate. By considering three fundamental factors - the quantities of four key chemical elements, the star formation patterns, and the velocities of stars within these galaxies - our model identifies the galactic types and histories that best match the observed data. Within the GSE system, our results indicate it was composed of two components with distinct chemical element compositions and varying masses, both following uniform star formation patterns. In contrast, the Wukong/LMS-1 system shows a more intricate variation in its chemical element compositions and we find two distinct sets of star formation patterns that closely resemble those predicted by our model. By comparing the velocities of stars within these galaxies to those predicted by our model, we validate the galactic escape velocity concept, providing further evidence that the GSE and Wukong/LMS-1 galaxies were indeed part of smaller galaxies that have since merged with the Milky Way. Our study marks a significant milestone in using abundance analysis and star formation pattern data to understand celestial body development and formation. This technique has vast potential for uncovering the hidden histories of various galaxies. Given our success with this method, we anticipate it will significantly contribute to future research in astrophysics. To facilitate this, we have released digital data containing all the information necessary for a thorough examination of the parameters used within our model. This data can be accessed via requests through the website http://galsim.org/. This allows for an unparalleled level of consistency and reproducibility, cementing the basis for a new approach in which galaxy reconstruction is achieved via detailed analysis of chemical element abundances and star formation patterns. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Our developed method is backed by an open-source library and extensive evaluation results, showcasing its effectiveness in a variety of real-world scenarios. Additionally, we have conducted thorough cost analyses to ensure that the simplicity of our selective labeling approach is tailored to the specific requirements of visually rich documents. Our approach aims to strike a balance between the costs of data labeling and model performance, empowering teams to make informed decisions about their use of active learning. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as formulating commands that are difficult to compute analytically. As a solution to this problem, we present a new algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient methods to tackle the numerical resolution of the CMDP. This approach, dubbed PDIT, both simplifies the command computation and effectively reduces the state and action dimensions by utilizing a primal-dual approach. Moreover, PDIT capitalizes on the structure of problem solutions by iterating on the value functions and policy until convergence is achieved. We apply our algorithm to two real-world SCMs: the first deals with the control of a inventory system with limited capacity, and the second covers the management of a vehicle routing problem with capacity constraints, both of which we illustrate with numerical examples. The results show that PDIT successfully resolves these problems within reasonable computation times, outperforming the existing Monte-Carlo sampling approach. The algorithm is open-sourced and available at https://github.com/marwani/pd-it-cmdp. This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism parameter tuning is eliminated. Our general Bayesian learning method can accommodate a range of models, including Bayesian linear and neural network models. Additionally, a variational inference algorithm is developed for efficient and scalable computations. The theoretical soundness of our approach is confirmed through established guarantees, which, along with simulations and real-world data tests, show our solution's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic investigations, and medical analyses. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, associated genes, and similar medical conditions. Yet, the conventional use of Euclidean distance measures is ill-suited to the binary nature of the data. A number of clustering approaches have been proposed to address this limitation, including the use of transformations such as the Pearson correlation coefficient or mutual information to represent similarity, or non-metric optimization techniques like the M-distribution or the Mants-approach to convert binary data into a real-valued distance measure. We examine a variety of these clustering methods including those based on Pearson correlation, mutual information, smoothings, Mants, and the general binary distance approach (GBDA) among others. These methods are compared through simulations and two case studies involving real data: one related to the analysis of ecological species groups and the other to clustering genes based on expression data. Our analysis considers both the stability and performance of these clustering methods. While some of these approaches, like Pearson's, rely on non-parametric assessment of the data, others - like the Mants-approach - are sensitive to the model assumptions formed during the clustering process. Our evaluation indicates that the GBDA and the STAN on real data performed well in both the simulations and the practical applications we considered. However, our study shows that the choice of the clustering method depends on specific research objectives and data characteristics. Consequently, a comprehensive set of clustering approaches should be considered to facilitate effective cluster analysis of presence-absence data. Additionally, our findings emphasize the importance of evaluating the robustness and clustering performance when selecting an appropriate method. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, the proposed iterative algorithm has been mathematically justified and verified with numerical experiments, which include real-world data obtained from a modified X-ray tube. The study demonstrates that this model can successfully counteract the distorting effects of beam hardening and electronic noise, ultimately enabling accurate reconstruction of the subject's underlying structure. Key outcomes include the accurate differentiation of Pecten Magister's brain and skull tissues from external background noises, and the identification of Aluminum cylinders within a geometric framework. Ultimately, this model is anticipated to significantly broaden the scope of CT applications, which may now include security screening and other scenarios involving multi-source X-ray beams. This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc. Additionally, this investigation leads to a conclusion about the compactness of the composition operator with a compactly supported continuous symbol (defined everywhere) on the Bergman space of the unit disc. Ultimately, this yields an equivalent condition for compactness of the composition operator with a compact symbol (defined everywhere) on the Bergman space of the unit disc. The central technique involves deriving upper bounds for the off-diagonal singular values of the composition operator with a compact symbol. Notably, this involves a novel application of a measure-theoretic concept known as Ahlfors' regulation theorem to estimate the growth of solutions to the inhomogeneous Cauchy-Riemann equations. Finally, this study provides a corollary that links the compactness of the composition operator with a compact symbol on the Bergman space of the unit disc to a related problem in multivariable complex analysis. Specifically, this compactness is equivalent to a stronger condition on the embedding of the image of a Jordan curve (within its boundary) into the image of a holomorphic function (based on L^2 norm). A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The derivation of the AdS amplitude allows us to recover the conformal field theory's twist-dimension spectrum as a function of 'zigzag' integrals, which exhibits asymptotic convergence and contains all-logarithmic terms up to the fifth order. Lastly, an evaluation of the preamplitude through the 'zigzag' integral is performed, yielding a result that can be related to the conformal field theory's anomalous dimensions via a scale change. In the case of operators with spin two, this approach yields a precise result that matches existing findings, while also providing an asymptotically convergent series expansion for the twist-four spectrum. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  Notably, DynaSOAr's approach is generally suitable for a range of applications, including SMMO programs, where it offers a range of options for domain-specific layout configurations, thus enabling users to trade off memory efficiency against performance based on their specific application needs.  Moving forward, we believe DynaSOAr will contribute to expanding the realm of parallelizable applications on SIMD devices, while its memory allocation and layout management techniques will also be useful for a range of other programming paradigms.  Ultimately, we hope DynaSOAr will inspire new research in this domain.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique, each utilizing a different technique to create the desired polarization entangled states: the first based on single photons and linear optics and the second using a two-mode squeezer. By examining both implementations and discussing the benefits and limitations of each, this research provides an understanding of entanglement preparation and its practical implications, highlighting an interface between diverse types of entangled states and potentially providing an alternative method for generating polarization entanglement through a heralded approach. By harnessing the advantages of both heralded and non-heralded entanglement preparation, this research could contribute significantly to the development of future quantum information processing applications. In particular, this research's findings on the generation of polarization entanglement could have an impact by overcoming some of the limitations associated with the non-heralded approach while still exploiting its advantages, thus paving the way for a versatile range of applications in quantum science and technology. Furthermore, this research also discusses how the proposed approach might be applied and extended within the context of notable quantum systems and experiments, such as those involving bosonic Tomonoes and quantum Gaussian circuits. By exploring these connections and considerations, this research could ultimately contribute to the advancement of entanglement research and development, while also revealing opportunities for further integration and innovation. Finally, we conclude by outlining some of these potential research directions and future avenues of inquiry, which could lead to the further development and dissemination of entanglement-based quantum research and technological applications. Keywords: Heralded approach, polarization entanglement, quantum scissors, continuous-variable entanglement, single-photon entanglement, two-mode squeezer. Important related concepts: quantum information, quantum information processing, optical quantum computing, quantum teleportation, quantum error correction, quantum circuits, quantum Gaussian circuits, bosonic Tomonoes, quantum Gaussian channels.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. These operators are then applied to provide an innovative approach to a specific class of random fields on the sphere, defined through one-dimensional functions, and facilitate a straightforward extension to random fields defined on compact manifolds of higher dimensions. The study provides an in-depth mathematical framework and exemplifies the proposed method by modeling a spatial correlation function for geophysical data, including a numerical verification based on the GeoGLEAM dataset. The 2D approach offers significant computational advantages and relatively minimal losses in precision over the direct evaluation of a 5-point Fourier hedge for the GeoGLEAM dataset. Additionally, it enables a straightforward extension to 3D and 4D random fields. The developed method can be utilized in numerous applications, including geophysical data interpretation, interpolation of missing values, and analyzing the spatial correlations of Earth's magnetic fields. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all this by leveraging the unique properties of a Michelson interferometer and combining it with induced coherence-based nonlinear interferometry, coupled with the use of a single-pixel imaging method. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. Our findings contribute to an comprehensive understanding of foam rheology and may also be applicable to other complex fluids. Moreover, this study may lead to new design concepts for materials, such as reduced-slip surfaces or self-cleaning materials, by exploiting the physics of "easy-slip" and "sticky-slip" states. We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio grows with time, specifically in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion, thereby resolving reported sublinear tendencies. The present study, along with our previous work on the two-state quantum walk, reveals that the participation ratio in quantum walks increases in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion. The underlying mechanics can be understood through system resolution using Fourier series. In contrast to claims in the literature, our results indicate that the participation ratio in the three-state quantum walk may directly relate to the first moment of the probability distribution, and this notion is experimentally verified using simulated data. The participation ratio's asymptotic value is found to be $2.41$ and the scaling function is derived, thereby enabling the estimation of the participation ratio at any given time and wavepacket spreading by simply inputting the survival probability and number of steps into the derived scaling function. Moreover, the participation ratio is shown to be dependent only on the system's size for large numbers of steps where wavepacket spreading is uniform. Based on the underlying periodicity, the system's size is estimated as $2.82$ and $4.18$ for the given coin operator parameters, respectively. The participation ratio is ultimately found to be a scaled multiple of the survival probability, thereby establishing a direct relationship between these metrics. The participation ratio can now be calculated using the survival probability and vice versa, thereby presenting new avenues for quantum algorithm analysis. The participation ratio can also be used as a metric to verify quantum walk-based quantum computing experiments where observing a transition from a localized to a fully dispersed wavepacket over multiple steps could demonstrate inherent probabilism in the experiment. The participation ratio can also be used as a metric in non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamic experiments where a transition from a localized to a fully dispersed wavepacket could be interpreted as a thermodynamic cycle where free energy can be calculated as the work done during this process and thereby establishing the possibility of doing work on the system as well as doing work by the system.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Building upon these insights, we developed the DINO self-supervised method, a form of self-distillation without the need for labelled data, and demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluating ViT-Base linearly. When fine-tuning ViT-Base linearly, we were able to achieve an 81.2% top-1 accuracy, surpassing the current best methods. Our work's contributions include introducing novel data augmentations and the DINO method, providing comprehensive ablation studies, and showcasing the robustness of our results on multiple datasets. Ultimately, we were able to transfer the acquired knowledge to downstream tasks, with experiments indicating an 11% improvement in the performance of ViT-Base/32 when utilized in the Darknet53 architecture. As such, our research sets a new standard for the field of self-supervised learning. The code for our research is publicly available at https://github.com/boeing-ai/дино.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. In contrast to several other studies on this topic, our proof avoids the use of Fourier restrictions and homogenization techniques, instead focusing on a straightforward calculation based on the structure of the equations and a well-known inequality related to the Strichartz estimates. The outcome of our study is a simplified proof that retains the original results stated by Bourgain and Li. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical aspects of the model's performance rely on the interpretation of uncertainty which is often underserved in deep learning models. This research introduces the use of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in reversible steganography, enabling more efficient exploitation of carrier image uncertainty. Our experiments demonstrate that BNNs offer a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art models. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/zhk500/BayesBNN_RVSteg. Our research presents an innovative approach to using BNNs in steganography, offering a versatile framework that can be applied across various predictive models to enhance the embedded capacity in reversible steganography. Utilizing the predictive distribution of BNNs, we design an efficient rate-distortion model that effectively exploits carrier image entropy in the presence of noise. This research offers an open-access framework comprising of BNNs and an enhanced rate-distortion model, both of which can be used to further develop state-of-the-art steganographic methods. Our findings show that BNNs offer a significant improvement over existing models both in terms of performance and computational complexity. Notably, the computational complexity of our model is comparable to that of the standard neural network approach. Nonetheless, the predictive distribution of BNNs enables our model to achieve a 0.5~0.6 dB improvement over the existing model with a comparable complexity. Moreover, our model facilitates the development of an iterative approach that effectively targets difficult-to-reach points in the rate-distortion curve. When compared with the current state-of-the-art iterative model, our approach exhibits a 0.5~0.6 dB improvement with a comparable computational cost. Conversely, our model demonstrates superior fidelity in the presence of the same computational cost as the existing model, thereby rendering it comparable in terms of complexity. Nevertheless, the existing model demands a complexity of at least twice that of our approach to achieve a 0.5~0.6 dB performance comparable to our approach. In summary, this research offers an efficient and computationally lightweight method for achieving high-quality steganography. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes more stringent limits on energy scales compared to other experiments such as beam dump, reactor, and meson decays. Furthermore, we discovered that J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter can be more sensitive to certain effective operators by a factor of several orders of magnitude or even two to three orders of magnitude in certain cases. Lastly, we found that J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter can be more sensitive to certain effective operators by a factor of six to seven orders of magnitude in the case of the D←C transition. Additionally, we found that J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter can be more sensitive to certain effective operators by a factor of six to seven orders of magnitude in the case of the D←C transition. This research demonstrates that J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter can be a highly sensitive test of both neutrino and dark matter interactions. In particular, it outperforms other experiments by a significant margin within their respective effective field theories. Therefore, it is essential to include J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter in the search for beyond the Standard Model physics. Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this understanding by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting the necessity of further developments in vision algorithms. Additionally,'minimal videos' offer a novel approach to investigating high-level visual processes and may provide valuable insights for developing more efficient computer vision systems. Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural geometries by minimizing congestion. The model adheres to partial differential equations that describe transportation based on molecular-motor-assisted models and is solved in complex tree structures through isogeometric analysis. We test our model by introducing different parameters that mimic traffic congestion, specifically investigating the effects of reduced microtubules and swirling structures on material transportation. Our simulations effectively demonstrate both the optimal material transportation in healthy neurons and the occurrence of congestion in neurons with abnormalities, illustrating the significance of both geometry and microtubule structure in facilitating optimal neural transport processes. Our approach provides a valuable tool for studying the optimal material transportation mechanisms in neurons with varying architectures and enables the investigation of the underlying causes of transportation-related congestion. Furthermore, this framework can be adapted for use in other complex branching structures, such as those found in other cells and in fluid dynamics. Given its versatility, this model can be applied across a range of fields to solve congestion-related issues resulting from traffic-like conditions, as well as other types of congestion resulting from reduced infrastructure or abnormal structures. Consequently, this model offers numerous possibilities for use in a wide range of applications. The approach described in this paper will be made available through an open-source software package as a pre-processed model that can be used for designing simulations based on user-specified neural structures and optimal transportation scenarios. Once released, this software will enable researchers to explore the causes and effects of congestion in neural transportation, as well as its implications in neural structures with varying geometry and microtubule composition. Consequently, this model will create new opportunities for using optimization models to design experiments and make informed decisions based on the optimal material transportation in complex biological systems. The software will include a comprehensive suite of tools for designing and simulating neural structures, as well as interpreting the results based on their topology. Moreover, it will incorporate a range of applications that demonstrate its versatility and offer new possibilities for use in a wide range of fields, such as modeling transportation in cells for better understanding of neurodegenerative diseases or other types of congestion-related issues. The open-source software package will be based on the open-source modeling language, GIMSChem, and will incorporate a range of algorithms for solving different models based on partial differential equations

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The outcome of our preliminary analysis indicates that extracting network motifs can reveal meaningful and understandable patterns within the data. Notably, our approach reveals a link between successful fraudsters and the use of network motifs, specifically those involving eight or more transactional nodes. Although the specific shapes of these motifs themselves do not directly correlate with fraudulent activities, they tend to appear more frequently at the top end of the fraud scale compared to the bottom end. When compared to the randomized control group, these motifs occur nearly five times more often in transactions involving fraudulent activities. Like needles in a haystack, extracting meaningful patterns from large datasets may require careful and careful analysis. In this study, we demonstrate that extracting network motifs can serve as a needle that points to the presence of fraudulent transactions within a given set. A comprehensive documentation of our methodology, including the code used in this research, is available at https://github.com/gsblb/nemovt. Additionally, the detailed flowchart of our analysis is available at https://github.com/gsblb/nemovt/tree/main/docs. This project is supported by the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council of Canada under grant number RGPIN-04195-2019. Lastly, we would like to express our gratitude to TD for collaborating with us, providing experimental data, and facilitating our research. In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern. Our analysis predicts a black hole mass range of 0.1 M_sun for these unique X-ray sources, and we propose that these systems could provide insights into the late stages of evolution of white dwarfs. Furthermore, our study suggests that binaries comprising zero-temperature white dwarfs and intermediate-mass black holes could emit similar bursts of radiation, potentially leading to new discoveries in the field. that arise from either camera motion or subject motion.  However, they often 
struggle to distinguish between different blur sources in real-world scenarios, 
leading to suboptimal outcomes.  To address this limitation, we introduce a 
multi-component system that separately generates and eliminates specific 
types of blur.  Our design begins by modeling a blurring agent using a 
conditional GAN-based synthesizer, which produces out-of-focus images based 
on the amount of blur.  Subsequently, we implement an advanced deblurring 
network that can reverse the effects of these synthesized blurs, thereby 
solving the original deblurring problem.  Through this approach, we enable our 
network to focus on specific blur types, thereby enhancing its ability to 
reproduce clear images in complex real-world situations.  As a result, our 
method outperforms the state-of-the-art by achieving higher PSNR and SSIM 
values on the MHD dataset, and producing more effective deblurring results 
based on user preferences.  Our implementation and dataset are publicly 
available.  Ultimately, the quality of our output matches human expectations 
by addressing specific blur types.  Therefore, we nickname this approach 
'Pseudo-blur Synthesizer'.  To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, 
we also introduce a multi-blur metric that quantifies the severity of 
multiples blurring sources in a single image.  Interestingly, we discovered 
using pseudo-blur synthesizer enables our method to focus specifically on 
addressing camera motion and subject motion separately.  To validate our 
assumption, we introduce an automatic metric called MBS score, which 
quantifies the severity of blur types.  Our MBS score suggests that our 
method is highly effective in removing specific blur types.  Our work 
contribution lies in two folds.  Firstly, we address a long-standing issue 
in motion deblurring research - distinguishing between different blur sources 
by modeling a blurring agent.  Secondly, we introduce an innovative use of 
blurring agents to focus specifically on removing camera motion and subject 
motion separately.  Our method is the first to achieve this distinction.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches rely on selective, model-agnostic testing, involving short sequences or synthetic data, which raises questions about the validity and representativeness of such benchmarks. In response, we propose the concept of dataset-specific profiling, which Involves running AI models on a reduced subset of a dataset, chosen using a heuristic tailored to the specific dataset at hand. We showcase the efficacy of this approach by profiling various models of object detection on the OpenIPTV dataset, demonstrating that this reduced subset is more relevant to the models and demonstrates a stronger correlation with their full dataset performance, while also revealing new insights about the dataset and model interactions. We make our profiling tool, called SubSim, available to the community to facilitate the evaluation of deep learning models on a wide range of scientific and industrial datasets. We envision a future in which dataset-specific profiling becomes a standard approach for evaluating models, leading to more accurate and effective results. We also perform an empirical analysis of the impact of dataset partitioning schemes on profiling outcomes, demonstrating that (1) different partitioning schemes can lead to disparate results; and (2) the quality of a partitioning scheme is directly tied to the quality of the corresponding dataset subset. We based our findings on an extensive evaluation of 10 distinct partitioning schemes, using multiple AI models, different dataset sizes, and varying model parameter counts. We also analyze how different AI model characteristics (e.g., architecture design, behavior, and interactions with the surrounding environment) affect their performance on a dataset, revealing that (1) different model types have distinct performance patterns; and (2) understanding these performance patterns can be harnessed to significantly improve subset selection. We use these results to guide the development of new dataset-specific profiling tools, and also provide recommendations for the design of novel profiling schemes, demonstrating along the way the benefits of addressing the uniqueness of specific datasets. We also study how different dataset subsets affect the training of deep learning models, revealing that (1) distinct subsets can lead to distinct model training outcomes; and (2) the quality of a subset is directly tied to the corresponding model training results. We use these findings to devise new profiling schemes that can prioritize models that excel on challenging data, and also develop novel strategies for selecting subsets that lead to uniform model training outcomes

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple settings in two scenarios: when working with incomplete tree annotations and when working with completely unstructured text. The results indicate that our approach can significantly enhance performance when annotated data is scarce, and surpass state-of-the-art results in several resource-constrained language scenarios. The code and models used in this research are freely available for public access at the link provided. This work is a direct extension of our previous study on neural parsing. Notably, our results show that Deep Contextualized Self-training can often outperform model fine-tuning using the BERT language model, a leading approach in the field, when working with limited, annotated data. Despite their superficial similarities, these two methods exhibit fundamentally distinct characteristics in terms of their reliance on external data, leading to the observed performance disparities. Ultimately, the choice between these approaches is dictated by the unique properties and constraints of the dataset at hand. Interestingly, our experiments show that both methods can contribute to improved parsing performance when used in sequence. In particular, we found that combining Deep Contextualized Self-training with BERT fine-tuning can lead to significant, synergistic performance gains. The maximum improvement achieved through this combination was found in the CoNLL2003 dataset, where Deep Contextualized Self-training had enhanced the parser's performance, and subsequent BERT fine-tuning had optimized the results, yielding a total gain of 2.3% in terms of the F-score. Similarly, in the CoNLL-X tags datasets, the combination of the two methods led to a total gain of 1.6% in the F-score. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' criteria as $p_n$ and $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$ through enumeration, and prove that $p_n \geq \frac{2}{5}$ when n is greater than or equal to 4 in an otherwise unmarked real-valued sequence. We also demonstrate that the previously established lower bound for $p_n$ can be further optimized to $p_n^* \leq 1 - \frac{1}{3^{n-1}}$ for n being at least 4 in an otherwise unmarked real-valued sequence. 

In our research, we identify the most general characteristics shared by triangles $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ that are both 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive'. We then explore potentially similar properties in higher-dimensional sequences, specifically examining the conditions under which a random n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ can be modified through a series of'monotonic' changes without altering the likelihood that it remains 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive'. We use this concept to create a game-like scenario, known as 'Cyclic', in which players' likelihood of winning can be lower than that of their counterparts in a related 'Transitive' game. Ultimately, our research offers a mathematical framework for understanding and analyzing 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' probabilities in sequences of n-tuples.

Previous studies have used recursive neural networks to estimate inter-beat intervals, but they have ignored the temporal properties of heart rhythms, leading to suboptimal performance. In an attempt to improve on this, we developed an innovative Tiramisu framework based on recurrent neural networks, and tested it against traditional recursive neural networks using data from the 2018 PhysioNet Cardiovascular Signal Processing Challenge. In addition to demonstrating the effectiveness of recurrent neural networks over recursive neural networks, we also proved the importance of using ECG signal segments with respect to heart rate to enhance signal estimation performance. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by solving
complex multi-task reinforcement learning challenges, such as navigating a
variable-level maze, in a variety of settings. Our research thus confirms that
using shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning
requires careful design to harness the benefits of representation learning.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the bath temperature and the scale factor. A broadly applicable geometric approach has been developed for these modified heat engines. The method involves converting the problem into a constrained minimization of the total entropy production within a time T, subject to restrictions on the heat released and scale factor applied. This is achieved through the utilization of a time-dependent scale factor in the system-bath interaction, resulting in optimal performance when its derivative resembles a sinusoidal function of time. The technique has been successfully demonstrated in two scenarios - an ideal gas in contact with an isothermal bath, and a van der Waals gas in contact with isothermal and isobaric baths. The application of this method to a specific type of gas in contact with an isothermal bath reveals the existence of a critical time T* above which the optimal entropy production decreases as a function of T, a phenomenon unattainable with time-homogeneous methods. Furthermore, this technique has been utilized to analyze the thermodynamic cycle of a Clausr-Purcell magic gate, illustrating its broader applicability to driven systems beyond classical thermodynamics. The calculation of the entropy production for an ideal gas in contact with an isothermal bath reveals that its maximum value follows a logarithmically correlated power-law, a phenomenon unobserved in time-homogeneous systems, and is likely to be encountered in various thermodynamic drives and heat engines under restricted control scenarios. The development of these novel geometric approaches to the analysis of driven quantum systems may provide valuable insights into the optimization of a wide range of thermodynamic drives and heat engines under restricted control, potentially leading to a wide array of applications in both quantum and classical domains. The techniques discussed here can potentially be extended to analyze the driven behavior of systems following a logarithmically correlated power-law and those exhibiting non-ergodic behavior, a possibility that may lead to further breakthroughs in the analysis of driven quantum systems. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, a comparison with state-of-the-art models shows the superiority of QPNet. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yunyao9986/QPNet. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed on the visible hemisphere of the Sun. Moreover, the spectral features were observed to shift towards longer wavelengths as the star's active regions rotate into view. These patterns were associated with the star's vector magnetic field and the uneven distribution of magnetic flux on the solar surface. These findings are crucial for distinguishing between planetary and artificial signals in solar data, and predicting the spectral features of actively rotating stars. Based on our investigation, the spectral features of superactive stars can be understood through the imposition of faculae on the solar spectrum, while the characteristics of stars with extremely strong magnetic fields are unpredictable. These studies are important for the optimal detection of other planets on the Sun and other G-type stars. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, a key method employed in this research involves formulating formulas for computing relative THH and MTHH maps, crucially including a universal coassociative comonad in THH, which facilitates the formulation of bicategorical traces. As a fundamental aspect, it is shown that these theoretical concepts are enforceable on the category of finite spectra, enabling a concrete understanding of shadows through the analysis of functors on the THH of the category of finite spectra. Finally, this research also constitutes a proof that shadows possess a functorial property, enabling the computation of homotopy categories of n-fold centralizers in the categories of finite spectra, by means of functors on the THH of the category of finite spectra. Lastly, a notable finding derived from this research is that homotopy theory contains an abundance of bicategories whose topological Hochschild homology exhibits a phenomenon known as non-trivial nilpotency, essentially meaning that homotopy theory is rich in sources of bicategorical shadows, which fail to be Morita invariants. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles can produce visually effective and unique results. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability, focusing instead on identifying a single optimal solution. In a deviation from the status quo, this study seeks to harness style-specific information, extracting it from image pairs to facilitate forward and reverse tone mapping. To achieve this, a novel neural network architecture is proposed, one that distills style from paired images and then employs it to map input images to their corresponding style-based outcomes, as well as reversing this process to recover input images from styled outputs. Through extensive experiments, the impact of distinct styles on the proposed approach was demonstrated, as well as its applicability to real-world image editing tasks via user interface examples. Ultimately, the implemented method was shown to be reversible and capable of achieving superior results compared to previous methods. The project's code and demo are openly available for inspection at https://danielneumann.github.io/style-disco.

This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon not seen in prior studies. Images captured within our study site show distinct vortex formations above the ground, creating areas of enhanced precipitation, supporting theories of preferential sweeping during snow settlement. These findings are a first in atmospheric turbulence research and may offer insights into the preferential sweeping phenomenon. Additionally, our research provides initial evidence of the accelerated snowfall velocities, awaiting further analysis to confirm its connection to the increased velocities of individual snowflakes. Although this study provides a first look at the preferential sweeping in the atmosphere, our research faces limitations in distinguishing between the effects of atmospheric turbulence and snowflake interaction. To address this, our research proposes several approaches for future study, including employing flow simulators to replicate the atmospheric conditions and recruit snowflakes from areas outside the influence of the snow surface. By addressing these limitations, our research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the preferential sweeping in the atmosphere. Lastly, our research offers essential insights into the accelerated snowfall velocities and the preferential sweeping, contributing to future developments in snowfall modeling and accelerated snowfall forecasting. These developments may ultimately aid in predicting and minimizing snow-related hazards, while also ensuring safe winter transportation and facilitating daily activities during heavy snowfall. Ultimately, our research seeks to bridge the knowledge gap between atmospheric turbulence and snow settlement, ultimately aiding in snowfall forecasting and management. To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons resulting from breakup, transfer, and incomplete fusion have been measured and calculated. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{51}$V system were experimentally measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with theoretical estimates obtained through calculations with the finite range coupled reaction method using the \textsc{FRESCO} code. Calculations indicated that the cross-sections from various reaction channels including 1n, 2n, 1p, 2p, 1s and 2s channels can be combined to form a total cross-section. This estimate showed good agreement with the experimental data, with estimated direct capture cross-sections indicating an overlap between incomplete fusion and breakup processes across the measured energy range. Furthermore, the relative proportions of different reaction channels including breakup into $\alpha$ plus deuterons, deuterons plus deuterons, and alpha particles plus protons, as well as 1p, 2p, 1s and 2s channels were derived from the theoretical estimates. It was observed that at energies above the Coulomb barrier, the breakup into $\alpha$ and deuterons is dominated by resonance-driven process, whereas across measured energies the process of Li breakup into protons and deuterons shows a different angular distribution compared to $\alpha$ production, indicating a distinct contribution from direct breakup process, with its contribution increasing with energy above the Coulomb barrier. A notable phenomenon was discovered where the process of Li breakup into deuterons and protons shows a forward peaked angular distribution at energies above the Coulomb barrier, unlike at energies below the Coulomb barrier where this process shows a random angular distribution. A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and standard wireless performance metrics like throughput and fairness. A bi-objective optimization approach combined with a deep learning framework provides the solution, allowing for the efficient scheduling of D2D links in mobile networks while meeting user quality of service requirements related to AoI. The proposed method is shown to yield optimal results compared to other techniques in various network scenarios. Additionally, the deep learning approach is found to significantly reduce the computational complexity of the scheduling problem. Key performance metrics like throughput, fairness, and generalized throughput fairness are presented to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed scheduling strategy. The code for this research is available on GitHub. This study offers a valuable contribution to the field of D2D communication via wireless links with non-trivial complexity. The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties. By adopting a requirements engineering approach, XAI can benefit from novel methodologies and techniques, such as stakeholder analysis, requirement elicitation, and requirement specification. These can help in identifying, prioritizing, and addressing explainability requirements that fulfill the diverse needs and expectations of XAI stakeholders. With this approach, requirements engineering contributes to the development of more transparent, understandable, and trusted AI systems by ensuring that their explainability needs are met. By integrating explainability requirements into the AI development process, stakeholders will have clearer expectations met regarding the explanations provided by these systems. In this way, the requirements engineering discipline contributes to the creation of explainability requirements that enhance the value of AI systems through the promotion of their transparency, reliability, and user-centric design. A case study on explaining image classification is used to demonstrate our proposed approach. This approach is novel and contributes to the advancement of research in explainable AI and requirements engineering. By promoting a user-centered design, this method fosters collaboration between XAI stakeholders to develop AI systems that are highly transparent, reliable, and easily understandable. Thus, this research offers a valuable contribution to both explainable AI and requirements engineering, with potential applications in a wide range of domains due to its versatile and generalizable nature. Key words: Explainable AI, XAI, Requirements Engineering, Explainability Requirements, AI Systems, Transparency, Trust, User-Centric Design, Stakeholder Analysis, Requirement Elicitation, Requirement Specification, Transparency, Reliability, User-Centric Design.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast amounts of labeled data, which is often scarce in the field of histopathology. We have developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 192,000 histological images aligned with relevant diagnostic information and annotated by experienced pathologists. This dataset facilitates the training, testing, and validation of machine learning models tailored to identifying and classifying colorectal polyps and determining the degree of dysplasia. Our goal is to contribute to the development of accurate and rapid diagnostic tools, enabling more efficient and effective medical procedures. We hope these resources will aid in advancing medical imaging research and ultimately translating these developments into clinical practice. The UniToPatho dataset is accessible and downloadable at: https://git.io/UnitoPatho. Supplemental materials are available at: https://www.unito.it/histo. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. In this study, our primary challenge is solving this maximal leakage problem for the case of a source with limited depth, where the source sequence is a random walk in a graph. For this problem, we develop efficient algorithms to find solutions, thereby providing clear bounds on the source size for any given level of leakage. The algorithms are further used to develop relaxation methods for the general case, where the adversary is allowed to make multiple guesses. The complexity of solving our relaxed problem is shown to be NP-hard for certain parameter settings, with our methods however offering significant performance improvements over brute force algorithms. The efficiency of our solutions is demonstrated in numerous experiments, where we also explore how our algorithms can be applied to other problems in coding theory, such as the problem of translating one code into another, with the goal of minimizing the adversary's guessing advantage. The development of efficient algorithms to solve this problem is seen as crucial to develop efficient source codes under the consideration of an intelligent adversary. With our approaches, we show that finding solutions to these problems is computationally feasible, thereby providing clear bounds on the size of the code. The adjacency matrix of the confusion graph, which encodes the distinctions between source symbols, is also used to develop a new criterion for evaluating the effectiveness of a given source coding strategy in limiting the adversary's guessing advantage. The importance of considering an intelligent adversary is then discussed in the context of real-world applications, such as data protection and data encryption, with our approaches offering a practical way to apply this consideration to problems in coding theory. Finally, our research is seen as a contribution to the broader field of learning theory, which studies how much information one system can gain about another system. With our investigation, we add to this body of knowledge by providing a detailed analysis of how much information a guessing adversary can gain in the context of zero-error source coding. The knowledge gained in our research is expected to be beneficial to applications in coding theory that consider an intelligent adversary

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  Moreover, we investigate how our approach handles noise during circuit operation, discovering that for short circuits it remains resistant to disturbances.  The outcome of these findings supports the use of the suggested method as an adaptable tool to exploit the mixed capabilities of QAOA within imperfect quantum devices. 

Keywords: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, Bayesian optimization, variational algorithms, quantum optimization, quantum circuits evaluation.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic formula to solve a resulting polynomial formed by combining the two ellipse equations, allowing for handling all cases of intersection points, including none, one, two, three, or four points. The proposed method has been implemented in C and validated through numerous tests with diverse input ellipses, demonstrating its efficiency for applications involving multiple overlap area calculations in simulations. We show that it can be learned via a simultaneous optimization approach using stochastic gradient descent, resulting in an efficient algorithm with linear convergence. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an end-to-end deep learning approach that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge about the spine to rectify and align the vertebrae, thereby facilitating accurate localization and identification. By integrating both global and local spine characteristics, this method can robustly handle internal spine deformities and external external factors (e.g., fixation hardware, acrylics, and artifacts) that often obstruct the spine and distort the CT images. To evaluate its effectiveness, this paper performs a comprehensive comparison of the proposed approach with other state-of-the-art deep learning methods, showcasing its superior performance on various datasets. I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. In this context, Galileo's influential status stems from his talent for clarifying the underlying principles of science in a logical and compelling manner, rather than from any significant innovations he brought to the scientific agenda. Nevertheless, it is significant that Galileo's efforts to demonstrate the scientific method's stability, as well as the significance of empirical research, helped to create an environment in which high-speed solar research could thrive. The intersection of strong experimental work and sophisticated mathematical tools ultimately gave rise to the scientific method used today, which is characterized by a continuous interplay between theoretical and experimental findings. The interplay between these two approaches can sometimes take the form of "one teaching, the other doing." The successful development of scientific work often depends not just on individual talent, but also on the unique contributions each person makes - whether it be Galileo's philosophical writing or the mathematical innovations of his colleagues. In this context, it is suggested that Galileo's role in history should be seen as that of a "mathematical amateur," whose considerable talents lay in illustrating the deep-seated principles of science through the lens of philosophy, while his colleagues continued to create new and groundbreaking mathematical concepts that in turn facilitated further scientific discovery and advancement. The steady progression of scientific progress was, in this view, driven by the interplay between Galileo's philosophical insights and the significant breakthroughs achieved by his mathematical colleagues whose contributions were, until recently, largely overlooked in the narrative of the scientific revolution.
